subtopic: UNITED STATES FRUIT CANNED IN CANADA AND EXPORTED

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: UNITED STATES FRUIT CANNED IN CANADA AND EXPORTED
speechtext:
A
Canadian Press dispatch from Hamilton. Ontario, carried in the local press this morning, under the headline "U. S. Fruit is Masked as Canadian Product." states that United States fruit is being canned in the dominion and exported to Great Britain under empire preferential tariffs. This charge .was made by delegates attending the Ontario Fruit Growers' meeting in Hamilton yesterday. Will the government give assurance to the house that these charges will be fully investigated at once and that such steps will be taken as may be necessary to ensure that the entire fruit content of each container of processed fruit exported to Great Britain is of empire origin?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: UNITED STATES FRUIT CANNED IN CANADA AND EXPORTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a letter was
addressed to me by the hon. member which, through no fault of his, did not come to my attention until just a moment or two before I entered the house.
My recollection is that the canners, at certain seasons of the year, when a supply is not available in this country, do import certain fruits for canning, which fruits are later exported. The rule, of course, is that in order to get the advantage of the preference in the British market there must be a certain percentage of Canadian content. I think it is fifty per cent, but I am not going to commit myself on that point because I am not quite certain on the point.
I need only say to the hon. member that I shall be very glad to make an investigation with regard to the matter.

speechtext:
There were two statements made by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) with regard to wheat and the actions of the government in relation to wheat, and that part of the trade agreement which has to do with wheat, and which I wish to comment upon for a few moments.
The first statement was that every bushel of United States wheat that goes into the British market replaces just that much Canadian wheat. I do not agree entirely with that statement. Every bushel of United States wheat that goes into the British market does not necessarily replace a bushel of Canadian wheat. Every exporting country in the world is attempting to enter the British market, and practically every exporting country in the world does enter the British market. The extent to which we are not able to compete with our United States friends and with all other producers of wheat throughout the world may and does have some effect upon the amount of wheat which we can sell in the British market, but every bushel of wheat that goes into the British market from the United States does not necessarily prevent a bushel of Canadian wheat from entering that market.
Reference was made by the hon. gentleman to the so called six-cent preference which we have on wheat entering the British market. Before going on to deal with this in detail may I say that when we were asked by the British government to consider releasing them from their obligation to give a six-cent preference to Canadian wheat, we were not the only country in the empire asked to do this. Australia was asked also, and Australia consented. Australia is the greatest competitor within the British empire that Canada has in the British market. Australia consented and Canada consented. Why did these countries consent? Because we realized that if these two countries could sell all their wheat in the British market, if there was no other country permitted to enter that market, then the six-cent preference might have some effect upon the sale of our wheat in that

However, the moment that either Australia or Canada has more wheat than it can sell in the British market, it must enter the world market in order to obtain a market for its wheat. Immediately we go into the world market outside of Great Britain we must accept the world price. I think everyone in this house will realize that in spite of sentiment the British always have been wise enough in a business way to buy their food products from the country in which they can get them cheapest, provided they are of the same quality. In other words, because of the good, hard business sense of the purchaser of wheat in Great Britain we. are forced on to the world market level. So far as we have been able to make out during the period this agreement has been in existence, the six-cent preference has not benefited the wheat growers of the western or any other part of Canada.

There is the question of how business going through our own Canadian ports will be affected.

I venture to suggest that the people of Saint John and Halifax, if they are to be affected by this argument at all, would much rather have the conditions prevailing in production, acreage and marketing where there is an annual shipment of 229,000,000 bushels through our ports rather than the 63,000,000 bushels that went through in the year when my hon. friend's percentage argument seemed to be a strong one.

speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend, but has he the figures of the Canadian wheat crop in those various years?

speechtext:
I have not the figures here, but I frankly admit that the crop has a
great deal to do with the figures, and that is the point I am trying to make, that the removal of the six-cer.t nreference has very little, if anything whatsoever, to do with the amount of wheat that is to be shipped through the maritime ports. As a matter of fact I looked up some other information which has a much greater bearing on the shipment of wheat through maritime ports than anything having to do with the six-cent preference, and this is the information I have. Most of the grain exported through Saint John and Halifax is drawn from Canadian bay ports and it is carried by water from the head of the lakes during the season of navigation. For a great many years past the Canadian railways, with respect to grain for export, have placed the ports of Saint John and Halifax on a footing of equality, so far as railway rates are concerned, with competing United States northern Atlantic ports-Boston, Portland and New York. In other words, you can ship wheat from bay ports on lake Huron for Halifax and Saint John for the same rate that you can ship wheat from Buffalo to United States ports on the Atlantic coast, and that will explain why a great deal of wheat under certain circumstances has gone through our Canadian ports. It is a special arrangement made through our board of transport commissioners and otherwise to give rates to our Canadian ports which will make it possible for wheat to pass through them. So that in addition to the crop figures in any particular year, you have this other factor which has a bearing on the shipment through Canadian ports.
And there is another which should be considered. Something was said the other day by way of comparison of the shipments through Canadian ports before the war and now. But in 1913 and 1914 the storage facilities in all the ports of Montreal, Quebec, Halifax and Saint John for the handling of wheat on the eastern borders of Canada amounted to only
9,000,000 bushels; in other words there were only 9,000,000 bushels of elevator storage in the harbours of eastern Canada in those years. In 1923 that had increased to 15,000,000 bushels, and quite a considerable part of that increased storage capacity was installed in the year 1922.
The Address-Mr. Gardiner

In 1928 there was space for 19,000,000 bushels and in 1938 for 21,000,000 bushels. I believe that that increase in the facilities, which was provided largely by the government under my right hon. leader during the time he was in power previously, had considerable to do with the increased shipments of wheat from our Atlantic coast, so far as it was not brought about by crop increases and otherwise during that period; and as my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) suggests to me, that is true particularly of the shipment of United States wheat. The facilities in our eastern ports to-day for the handling of wheat are much greater than they were before the war.
Something has been said with regard to the effect generally upon business of anything that might decrease the shipment of our wheat through these particular Canadian ports. I have in my hand a copy of an article published in the St. John Telegraph-Journal of January 10, 1939, which contains several columns of comment on this very question, but the only passage I shall quote reads as follows:
But, as stated, freight follows grain; and if St. John is to hold her place in world trade traffic, all the available pressure must be brought to bear now.
The federal government has bonused western farmers, at a cost estimated at $60,000,000, guaranteeing the price of eighty cents per bushel for grain which to-day sells for sixtyfive cents.
They go on to argue that because of that, and because of the importance of wheat to business in our Atlantic ports, the government of Canada should do something to see to it that wheat goes through our Canadian ports. The point I wish to emphasize in connection with that statement is that wheat is not only of great importance to Halifax, Quebec, Saint John and Montreal, but it is equally important in the business build-up of cities like Fort William, and of a city like Vancouver on our western coast. It is just as important to Vancouver as it is to any of these cities on the Atlantic coast that are mentioned in this article. In other words, as has been stated time and again in this house and throughout the country, wheat produced in the central part of this continent to be shipped to the importing countries of the world is a commodity that affects the whole financial set-up and business set-up of this country; and because of that, there are certain arguments that can be adduced with respect to this particular commodity that do not apply with nearly the same force to some other commodities.
I have not time to deal further with the question of wheat to-day; in any event there are so many resolutions on the subject on 
the order paper that I do not think it is necessary for me to say more at the moment. But I have put this information on Hansard so that it will be available to any member of the house who wishes to have it.
There has been some discussion since this debate opened as to whether the policy of the government was sound when we contended prior to the last election-and we have followed that policy since-that trade has a great deal to do with the settlement of unemployment and other problems having to do with the development of the Dominion of Canada. The argument was summed up by the leader of the opposition the other day somewhat to this effect, that under our agreement with the United States we were paying $40 per head for what we purchased from the United States while they were purchasing goods from this country to the extent of only $3.50 per head. Now if we followed that argument to its logical conclusion we in Canada would have to sell $2,400 worth of Canadian products per family in order that the Americans might be on the same per capita basis as the Canadians who are purchasing goods from the United States. In other words the argument of my hon. friend is reduced to ridiculous proportions.

speechtext: Why not have the Americans increase their purchases?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
He started out to argue that the United States should purchase from us per capita as much as we purchase per capita from them. We, being the smaller country of the two, a country in its stage of development, a country producing great quantities of natural products which are consumed by a dense population, naturally sell a great deal to the American people; but if my hon. friend wants us to sell as much to
130,000,000 people per capita as they sell to us per capita, with our 11,000,000 people, the United States would have to buy $2,400 worth of goods from every family in the Dominion of Canada. If my hon. friend works out the figures he will find that that is correct. Anyone who follows out the argument knows that while that might be desirable for Canada, so far as the United States is concerned it would be an absolute absurdity.
Then we have the question raised whether this is a matter which could settle our unemployment problem, or whether the world situation to-day has had the effect upon our unemployment which we as a government maintain it has. I would call attention to the fact that experiences such as the present are not new. We had a similar experience

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
just fifty years ago; we had another twenty-five years ago, and on each of these occasions exactly the same results ensued as those produced by the influences of this present period. The other day I picked up a copy of a western paper which was edited fifty years ago by a gentleman who either at that period or a little later was a member of this house, and I was surprised to find in it this statement, in the editorial column-this relates to the year 1888:
From this distance war in Europe seems inevitable. War is a dreadful curse, yet it will put up the price of wheat.
Fifty years ago they were talking about the same influence as we have been talking about in these recent months.
A dispatch from Rome said France must sooner or later endeavour to break the iron circle in which the unity of Italy and Germany has bound her.
That statement is identical to one which might be seen on the front pages or in the editorial columns of a newspaper to-day. And everyone who remembers the eight-year period from 1888 to 1896, about the same in point of duration as the period of stress through which we have just passed, recalls that the conditions were similar to those we have just experienced. Unemployment was just as rife, unemployment camps were just as numerous, people were getting lower wages and lower prices than we are getting now.
But, not to prolong the argument as to what happened fifty years ago,, let us come down to twenty-five years ago. I ran my first election campaign in 1914, in the period immediately preceding the war, and I recall that the arguments at that time were similar to the arguments we hear now. I recall that in June of 1914 young men were sitting on the curbstones of the city of Regina and elsewhere waiting for jobs, in a period when we still had homesteads available in the western part of Canada. I recall that very shortly after that a disturbance arose which had been threatening the world for two and a half years and which convinced us as to what was the cause of unemployment. And recently, within the memory of everyone who is sitting in this house, no matter how young he may be, we have had proved to us that there has been an accumulation of causes leading to a similar result which was staved off in September of last year only by the efforts of Mr. Chamberlain, the Prime Minister of Great Britain. Knowing that, we are convinced that the greatest problem which confronts the people of the world to-day is that of maintaining the peace of the world. I have said on a previous occasion, and I repeat it now, that if the world could be assured of peace during our
generation unemployment as a national problem would sink into insignificance inside of twelve months. Some of my friends of the opposition have twitted me with trying to explain away or in some way to remove from this government any responsibility it has in the matter of dealing with unemployment. If they tell me that trade has nothing to do with unemployment I will again place on Hansard the figures with regard to this matter. The figures are for December of each year:

There is only one other matter I want to deal with, and it has to do with comments of a more or less personal nature. I would not have referred to the matter at all had the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) not made this particular statement. At page 48 of Hansard he is reported as having said:
Do I draw the conclusion that he was trying to flimflam Mr. Hepburn? He is supposed to be a friend of Mr. Hepburn. The talk is that he was one of the men mixed up with Mitchell in an attempt to overthrow this government. That was the kind of talk.

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
And then I am asked whether I am a friend of Mr. Hepburn's. Well, I hope I am; that is a question only he can answer, but that does not mean that I must follow all my friends in all the courses they may map out for themselves. I should hope too that I am a friend of the leader of the opposition. I have known him, not intimately, but slightly, for some years and I hope I am a friend of his. But I trust the good Lord will preserve me from travelling the devious political routes which he has found it necessary to follow to reach his present position. I do not think it necessary that in order to be a friend of any person I should follow that person all the way in every direction in which he may desire to go in connection with political or any other matters. I do hope, however, that I can still sit down and discuss, both from another man's point of view and from the standpoint of the future welfare of the country, at any time, any question that may arise. I would even do so with my hon. friend in the hope of being able to convince him that he should come back to his first love. He says:
The talk is that he was one of the men mixed up with Mitchell in an attempt to overthrow this government.
I simply wish to make this statement finally. I have been in the public life of Canada since 1911. I have been a member of a house either provincially or federally for the last twenty-five years and I consider that in that time the highlights of the political life of Canada were 1911, 1917, 1929, so far as I am concerned, and 1934 as a completion of the experience. As early as 1911 those of us who sit on this side of the house had to make up our minds whether or not we were in favour of trade arrangements with great countries like the United States, and we made up our minds in spite of the fact that the majority of the people of the country did not agree with us at that time. We are pleased, however, to find them in agreement with us now.
Again, in 1917 as a member of the Liberal party I had to make up my mind whether I was going to follow the grand old leader of the party or do what looked like the best and easiest thing for the time being. I decided, Mr. Speaker, that whatever the future might have in store, I was compelled on that occasion to stand for the principles that he had taught me to believe in, and I stood by the leader of the party of that particular day.
Then in 1929, as the leader of a party in a province, I had to make up my mind whether I would throw down a mere minority on a matter of principle, or whether I would submit to defeat, and I adhered to principle and took defeat, with the result that the people of Saskatchewan said in 1934, what they were not

successful in saying in 1929, that they were prepared to wipe out the entire support of the principles that were put up in opposition to us in the election of 1929.
In other words I have found from my experience that it is a good thing to stand by principle. Personalities do not mean so very much in politics. Individual men do not mean so much in themselves. We happen to be fortunate on this side of the house in having our present leader. Someone said the other day that he was so much engaged in external matters that he had not time to deal with internal affairs. Well, I have learned to follow the leader of the Liberal party in Canada to-day because I know that when we are confronted, as we were in September, with one of the greatest crises that can face this world, we have the one man in Canada who is most capable of handling the situation to the satisfaction of the people.
Let me say this to my hon. friend. If ever I find it necessary to try to defeat a government in Canada I will try to defeat it from the outside. While I sit on the treasury benches of the dominion or of any province, any one who is writing editorials or taking any other action in connection with politics will be wise to check up the records. If he does he will come to the conclusion that I shall stay with the principles of the party no matter if the ship sinks. And I will say further that if ever I wish to oppose the government of Canada of which I have been a member I will do what my hon. friend from Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) did-I will leave the government, I will resign, I will relinquish the emoluments of office and go to the country and fight for the principles in which I believe. But if some friend should leave, I will not remain in the government until the people of the country defeat the government to which I belong, leaving the impression I am in agreement, and then say that my hon. friend was right by taking him back and having him sit on my right hand in this house.
. The position which we hold as a party in the Dominion of Canada, if we really acknowledge the trust that has been placed in us, is one that calls upon us to support principle, to support leadership, so long as it stands for principle, and to go down to defeat for principle if necessity requires it.

The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who has just preceded me, will pardon me if I do not follow him in all the variations of his argument. However, I am delighted to find at last that he and I have something in common, because I observe from the last

The Address-Mr. Rowe (Dufferin)
part of his speech, when he told the house the story of his life, that he met defeat in his life as I did in my native province.
I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews) and the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier) on the excellent speeches they made in moving and seconding respectively the speech from the throne. I am also glad to say that I express the truest sentiments of the people of Dufferin-Simcoe when I say that it was with genuine pleasure and sincere delight that I heard in the speech from the throne of the proposed visit to Canada of Their Majesties the King and Queen. I know that every citizen in my riding is filled with renewed British pride and security and hope as he anticipates the unique occasion of this proposed royal visit. When one listens, in this section of the empire, to those who underrate our British institutions, to those who prefer the red flag to the union jack, to those who would choose the "isms" of another people, and to those who would make our national security dependent upou foreign relationships, one may very well say that the proposed visit is not only timely and appropriate but almost a necessity. I hope that visit may bring pleasure to their majesties and inspiration to Canada. I hope our people, as they pray God Save the King, may in turn resolve to save this Canada as part of the great British empire. I feel sure that this visit will renew, in no small degree, our pride in our own country and, in a greater degree, bring renewed confidence in our own empire.
I regret, Mr. Speaker, that we are about to lose from this house one of Canada's most colourful statesmen, Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. It has been my pleasure and privilege to follow him during all his years of service as our leader on this side of the house, and I know his departure will be a loss to parliament and to the country. However, I am delighted to congratulate the hon. member for London (Mr. Manion) who has assumed the great task of Leader of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition. He brings to his task an excellent character, a unique personality and splendid ability. He represents true Canadian life. In every activity in which he has engaged he has been a star performer. He excelled in the field of sports; he excelled in the field of learning; he was decorated on the field of battle and he has been made a king's privy councillor in the field of parliamentary activity. I am satisfied that he brings to his task the qualifications to make not only a splendid leader of this party but an excellent prime minister of this dominion. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) smiles, but may I advise him that it will not be long now.

speechtext:
I think I have mentioned the chief feature of the speech from the throne, that is, the announcement of the visit of their majesties; because even you, Mr. Speaker, will agree that the remainder of the speech from the throne is a somewhat tiresome document, written by his majesty's advisers who sit to your right. It is pretty well filled with the glittering generalities which have epitomized the political skill of the Prime Minister for a long time, and it brings very little relief to the people of this dominion. It mentions matters of defence, trade treaty policies and unemployment, but that mention only reminds the people of Canada of the insecurity, instability and uncertainty that surround those issues to-day. The remainder of the speech is made up of gestures, and excuses, before a new election, for promises which were made before an old election.
I cannot help but think, Mr. Speaker, that the reference to our defence policies does little to remove the insecurity that surrounds that issue in the minds of the Canadian people. I would like to commend the government, however, for their declared intention to remove the profits from the manufacture of munitions. Even though it is a year late I believe that is a most commendable step to take at the present time, and I am satisfied that the government will receive support from this side of the house in any effort that may be made to control such blood money in these difficult times. However, I do feel that the people of this country, in connection with defence, are not concerned so much with the details of a certain contract or even the general details of the defence department. I believe our people are more concerned with the details of a definite national defence policy for Canada. I have not heard any hon. member to your right, Mr. Speaker, tell us where this defence policy might lead if an unfortunate crisis should arise. They have not told us that they stand shoulder to shoulder with the British Empire; and just yesterday in another place we heard the government leaders state that they were not even sure that the old land would stand by us.
I think it only fair to ask whether our defence policy is as strong as some may

The Address-Mr. Rowe (Dufjerin)
assume it to be. It is not nearly as strong, I submit, as it should be. I do not want to be misunderstood. I will support this government if they spend two dollars for every one dollar they are now spending in connection with defence. I believe that in the past all governments failed to assume their proper share of responsibility in connection with preparing for any crisis that might arise, a crisis that in these days sometimes seems almost inevitable. I sometimes think it would be better to spend more, knowing where we were going, rather than less if we did not know where we would be when the need did come. Is ours to be a more or less imaginary, independent defence policy? Is it to depend for its chief source of strength on some magic plan of economic appeasement to avoid attack; or in time of trouble is it going to be clearly in line with that of the friendly country to the south; or will it consist of closer cooperation with the mother country? I do not know the reason for all this mystery that surrounds this important department. One often wonders if a policy of this kind can be maintained as a political convenience for an era of peace without defining upon whom we are going to depend if an era of war should arrive.
I have already stated that the trade treaties of this government do very little to remove the instability and insecurity which exists to-day in regard to trade matters. I regret to say that I have not much confidence in the government opposite in regard to fiscal matters. I have seen them in action and I think I understand the tendencies of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. I saw his party in power before 1929. I saw them in opposition in more difficult days, and now I have seen them in power for the last four years. I well recall the number of trade agreements that were brought into this house between 1925 and 1929. We were told that they would give the farmers higher prices for their products and allow them to buy where they could buy the cheapest. And I recall that in almost every instance those agreements opened the gates wider for the importation of cheap finished products, sweatshop articles produced in foreign countries, at the same time facilitating the export of raw and unfinished products from Canada. It. has been my privilege to observe these things at close range, so I cannot help it if I am a little suspicious at the present time.
I was amazed to hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) suggest to-day that because we have fewer people we should buy

more than the United States buy from us, with their much greater population; and having large resources we should allow them to sell us more than we should hope to sell them. I could not help thinking, "Oh for the days of 1911." Unfortunately I was not able to vote, but I thank the Lord that reciprocity was defeated without me: I cannot help recalling the arguments laid before us in those days. We were told how 120,000,000 people- probably it was about 115,000,000 then- would buy so much from 10,000,000 people, and that we could hope for a great development. I recall also the tendencies of trade and the fiscal policy of the administration in those years. I cannot help recalling that before 1929 the government of that day rode on the crest of prosperity throughout the world and derived the advantages of bountiful harvests at home. As the minister to-day made his argument which he hoped the maritime people would read, I could not help thinking that the maritime people would be surprised to find him comparing drought years with bountiful years.
During those years the government boasted of prosperity, and yet it failed to give employment to our own people. I recall that the government's fiscal policies between 1921 and 1929 left us, in the latter year, at a point where we were buying a million dollars worth of goods every day the sun rose, goods of a class or kind our own workmen could have manufactured, more than we were selling. To no small extent that is the reason why between the years 1921 and 1930, the time to which the government to which the minister has referred held office, more people left Canada to find employment in the United States than were bom in this country.
What further evidence could we have of the weakness of a fiscal policy which could not survive even in days of bountiful harvest and world prosperity? Yet to-day we are asked to believe that this same policy of fiscal laissez-faire will bring about economic appeasement which will make all well. The Minister of Agriculture pleads of course for world peace. The Prime Minister prays for world peace and good weather, in order to bring back prosperity as in years past. We were told during those years that we must not provoke the United States. We are now told that we must take the lead and show the magic way by a new plan of economic appeasement. We are told we must make our tariffs lower than those of any other country, and all this during the most highly competitive industrial period of our age.
It is not my purpose on this occasion to review at length the Canada-United States

The Address-Mr. Rowe (Dufferin)
agreement. I do feel however that I must make some observation to indicate how it appears to me. We are told by the Prime Minister that the agreement will be brought down in the near future. I cannot help thinking that the Canadian people as yet have not studied it carefully. The doubt I entertain as to the treaty-making ability of the party sitting to your right, Mr. Speaker, is not relieved to-day. I view the proposed treaty with much more alarm than I should like to express.
I observe that last year we bought from the United States $130,000,000 worth more of goods than we had bought the year before of a class or kind which could be made by our workmen who are tramping the streets today. This condition to no small extent can be traced to the weakness of the trade agreement of 1935. For that reason I am asking how we can have much confidence when we view the agreement and find it is proposed to reduce the tariffs to a point lower than that which obtained in 1935. Not only is the tariff placed at a point lower than it was placed in 1935, but it is reduced on a greater volume of goods. The United States can reduce its tariff only to the extent of fifty per cent. We lower ours all the way along the line, and all for fear we may provoke them and for the purpose of developing this great policy of economic appeasement.
I observe the three per cent excise tax is removed from the produce of United States manufacturers, but the eight per cent sales tax is left on the Canadian manufacturers. One cannot help but view with alarm thr advantages gained under the treaty by twenty five or twenty-six other countries under thi= most favoured nation provision. These advantages are given to the sweatshops and cheap products of other countries and there is very little hope for a quid pro quo.
As a farmer I can see very little advantage for the apple growers in the east or the fruit and vegetable growers in the central part of Canada. Not only do they lose advantages in the British market but under the proposed treaty they will meet new competition in their own. I can imagine the advantages which will be paraded before the producers of western Canada by the Minister of Agriculture. The producer will be told that he can ship more cattle than he could last year. But that producer will find that by a peculiarly smart provision he has a larger quota when he has less to sell and a lesser quota when he has more to sell.
To my mind the treaty bristles with dangers, bristles with possible destruction for the major industry of Canada, and offers very little to the other primary industries. As I see it, it is
a sacrifice on the altar of a so-called economic appeasement. It sacrifices the great advantages gained in the empire agreements of 1932 and accentuates the weaknesses of the 1935 agreement with the United States. It surrenders jobs to United States workmen and forfeits the three per cent excise tax so sadly needed for our revenue. Yet we are told that we should support it, because it is a step towards the economic appeasement of the world.
These are only a few of the first impressions I have gathered from the proposed treaty. In the light of the government's record I would say that the most alarming feature is the basis of fear upon which the treaty seems to have been made. Do not let us confuse the issue. Sound and solid trade policies in Canada have never in the past and will not in the future interfere with or prejudice our friendly relations with the great republic to the south. Do not let anyone camouflage the issue by telling us that until we give the people of the United States everything they want they will be provoked. There seems to be a suggestion that we should throw down our barriers to permit the sale of mass production from the United States, in order that we may get our raw products into that market so that they may fabricate them. The suggestion is dial unless we do that we will be guilty of some form of provocation or that we will not be working towards economic appeasement and that we will be endangering those cherished and friendly relations which we have long had and no doubt will continue to have, no matter what type of policy we may pursue.
We might just as well say that the spineless and haphazard fiscal policies of this government would soften the stubborn and heartless military policies of some European dictatorships. We might as well say that you must give everything, if you are going to have peace, even with a friendly country. The economic appeasement of the world is a high and lofty motive. I commend the Prime Minister upon having made that reference. But as long as we have ablebodied men in Canada pleading for jobs to restore their morale, men whose wives should be spending more earned money and thereby improving our prosperity, I say that our first duty as Canadian public men is towards the economic appeasement of the idle men in Canada.
This brings me to the subject of unemployment. The Minister of Agriculture has said that in those years when we had great prosperity only 100,000 or so were unemployed. I can remember the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) stating, I believe in 1928, that 1,100,000 men had left this country between 1920 and 1930 to find employment.

The Address-Mr. Rowe (Dufjerin)
The hon. member says there were only 100,000 left at home that were unemployed. Why should there be any unemployed after all the boasting of prosperity that we heard?
May I remind him that during the years 1931, 1932 and 1933, when the party to which I have the honour to belong was being condemned and criticized by the opposition because there were a few hundred thousand unemployed in Canada, according to a return by a department in Washington over 400,000 Canadians who had gone to that country to find jobs had returned to Canada and no more were being allowed to enter. Why would we not have unemployment?
Unemployment is a condition that gnaws at the very heart of this young dominion. I was disappointed the other day when I read a speech made in Montreal by the Minister of Agriculture. He said that fundamentally we had no unemployment problem at all. I could not help thinking of the days that are gone and the years that are past when I sat in this house and heard the present Prime Minister say in 1930 that there was no unemployment. Yfet we have the Minister of Agriculture stating now that there were a hundred thousand unemployed. Just a few days after the Prime Minister made that statement he had to call out the militia and the horse guards to keep them away from the front of the parliament buildings. They did not see the problem then and they do not see it now.
This is and has been a national problem. The man who first saw it as a national problem was the former leader of this party, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Bennett). He recognized it as a national problem and in 1930 called a special session to deal with it as such. However, I think he would be the first to admit that perhaps he did not go as far as he should have gone at that time. Since 1929, since unemployment was assumed as a national problem, we have spent one billion dollars. What for? To give direct and work relief. But we have not even touched the real problem itself. We are waiting for the fears of war to disappear, we are waiting for bountiful crops, we are waiting for the curtailment of wheat production in other countries; we are trusting to the peace of the world and the Lord of the weather. We are relying too much on the policy of laissez-faire and do nothing.
It is no longer a problem merely of dealing with the man or the woman who is unable to work. That problem was dealt with long ago. Even Queen Elizabeth with her poor laws gave relief in 1601 to the poor people who

were unable to work. This problem is not one of direct relief, but it is the direct responsibility of the national government. It is a problem not confined to the boundaries of our own nation but one that goes into international circles. It is not a matter of dealing with poor people who are unable to work; it is a matter of providing employment for the employable men and women of Canada.
A commission was set up by this government to investigate the labour situation. Every time this government is faced with a problem it appoints a commission and prays that there will be an election before any action has to be taken. To my mind it is most important and essential that the major aspects of the relief problem should be dealt with by this government. No longer can the government rest upon its oars and say the municipalities should deal with this form of aid. The municipalities can deal with those who are unable to work, but responsibility must be assumed by this government for those who are able to work. We must differentiate between the two. We must have a new outlook on the unemployment situation. It is national in scope and it should be a national responsibility. The provincial governments may be left to deal with those who are unemployable, with those who are unable to work, but the larger issue of employment should be met by national measures. It should be under national control and be assumed as a national responsibility.
I hope that before another election comes around this government will be prepared to assume responsibility rather than continue to dodge the issue. We hear there is to be an unemployment insurance policy for Canada. I submit that the people of this country do not want an unemployment insurance policy, they want an employment assurance policy. That is what our people need. We want the assurance of work for our people rather than insurance against defeat and relief. We take out insurance against damage by hail, by storms, against death and so on. Perhaps that is why this government is suggesting an unemployment insurance plan. Apparently they admit the death of the issue, apparently they realize the hopelessness of it all unless the weather changes and the peace clouds rise.
I could elaborate upon this if I had more time. There are national advantages that lie behind an employment assurance plan and there are dangers that bristle in an unemployment insurance plan. One of the great dangers in relief is the loss of morale and initiative by those who accept relief for nothing. This problem should be fitted into the fiscal policy

The Address-Mr. Rowe (Duflerin)
of the government as well as any public works plan. There should be some recognition of the problem by the dominion and the provincial governments. I regret that at the present time it is being found quite difficult to have a friendly conference by the so-called happy family of Liberalism as it is constituted in disunity to-day. I am glad the Minister of Agriculture has said that all is well and that this danger is soon to disappear.
If the government recognizes this problem as I have indicated it sketchily there will have to be a readjustment in the revenues of the dominion and the provinces. Everyone who has any knowledge of industry and finance knows something of the inequitable burdens imposed by the many variations of duplicate taxation. No doubt the adoption of a national employment assurance policy would require some adjustment in the revenues of the provinces. I do not want the Prime Minister to think that I am critical of everything he does, because I have seen him do some things that would have been, done even by the leader of the opposition. However, I do suggest to him that I believe the time has come when we should deal with this matter as a national problem. Consideration should be given to national revenues in order that this national emergency may be met. In this connection I would suggest that all income tax be placed under the federal authority. More than that, the stock transfer tax and the corporation tax might well be transferred to one central body. I do feel that if that were done and the federal government assumed full responsibility for a national employment assurance scheme, our people would be satisfied to meet the obligations it would involve.
Income taxes more than any other form of tax should be used for the protection of income. In other words, the mass income of the earning . people of Canada may very properly be the bulwark protecting income for the employable masses of Canada. If my proposals were accepted, which would involve the income tax being more broadly based than it is at the present time, and those earning income in Canada had an opportunity to contribute to such a plan of national employment assurance, I believe that no one would be averse to making an income tax contribution to a sound national employment assurance plan applicable throughout this dominion.
I do not want to be understood as suggesting that this should be the only tax to be diverted to the federal treasury, although I suggest it is the most important one; I believe that the other taxes I have mentioned
might well be considered in this connection. I do not wish to labour the point as to what advantages would accrue, but I know that there are few in business or industry to-day who would not say that it would be a great relief if they even paid the same amount of tax as they do to-day into one central fund rather than to half a dozen different sources. If some definite effort were made by the government along this line it would go a long way towards encouraging industry.
I consider that the capital and earnings of industry other than those paid in salaries, wages and dividends, should be free so far as possible from tax impositions in order that some of the shackles may be removed from industrial enterprise and national expansion.
The adoption of such a policy would not only be a step in the direction of doing away with the duplication of taxation that exists to-day, but would mean a corresponding saving in the cost of administration.
There might be some objections, it is true, from those who believe that we are centralizing too much authority in the federal government. But I do not believe it ever was the intention of the fathers of confederation that we should be nine sovereign states within a state. It was never their intention that the provinces should flout and exploit the very basic sovereignty of their autonomous rights. I do not believe that a limited centralization of authority along some of the lines that I have suggested would constitute any premature centralization that might aggravate the disharmonies inherent in a federation. The whole system seems to me to have grown almost out of hand. It was not expected that the provinces should surrender their sovereign rights, but I believe that the fathers of confederation intended much to be left to the good sense of the men they hoped would be in power, knowing that there must be some things that are definitely federal in character and others definitely provincial. I do not believe you can wipe out functions that are definitely provincial, but there are certain forms of taxation that should be centralized in the central body, for primary and productive efforts. There are certain functions that are definitely provincial, and others that are definitely national in character and which must always be considered a dominion responsibility.
I believe the government should give careful consideration not only to a plan of national employment assurance but to plans for reducing the cost of government in so far as our constitutional machinery will permit. There is only one way in which

The Address-Mr. Rowe (Dufferin)
it can be done and that is by the time-honoured British custom of conference, compromise and conciliation between the provinces and the dominion, and I want to compliment the Prime Minister in this connection. I believe that he has excellent ability and can achieve something through conference, compromise and conciliation between the provinces and the dominion. I hope that something along that line will be done in order to bring about a more friendly relationship between the provinces, to show the way to those who are to-day confused by the present duplication of taxation, to give hope to those who are tired of waiting for jobs and relief to those who are disappointed in the present lack of action.
I can conceive of no plan or ideal of national service that is more necessary at the present time or more worthy of a democratic people than something along these lines. I can conceive of no national policy which would more effectively protect, encourage and develop the ideals of democracy than one which will gainfully employ our people and thereby assist them to reestablish themselves-a policy that will give gainful employment to those who seek jobs, a type of employment that will enable the family spending their earned income to keep their self-respect. I think that is the only way in which we can hope to restore confidence in our institutions and in national leadership.
The people of this country are pleading to-day for a national policy. They are pleading for a national hope, for a release from a policy of laissez-faire and do-nothing, before doubt, discontent and disunity further threaten the progress which our people desire.
May I commend to the government and their supporters, and especially to the Minister of Agriculture, who I regret is not in his seat at the moment, the issue of the Financial Post of January 7 last, where they will find, neatly compiled, editorial comment from newspapers representing districts both of our near east and the far west. Among these are-

I do not wish to trespass beyond my time, Mr. Speaker, but if I have the consent of the house I shall take only a moment to finish. I hope that the government will read this
[Mr. W. E. Rowe.)
editorial comment in the Financial Post coming from newspapers representing practically all sections of Canada and including the Toronto Telegram, Fort Erie Times Review, North Bay Nugget, Brantford Expositor, Winnipeg Free Press, Northern Pas, Saskatoon Star, Calgary Albertan, Swift Current Sun and Prince Rupert News. I shall quote only a short extract or two.
The Prince Rupert News "sees all faces turned to Ottawa for action." It recalls that Laurier did not have to be prodded into action but that the present Prime Minister seems to be lagging in leadership. It says:
What the country sees to-day is that many people are idle, and having no Liberal leader, they are listening to subversive leaders who will destroy them as those who followed the [DOT] pied piper were destroyed.
The Swift Current Sun speaks in similar vein. It refers especially to the vicious, demoralizing influence of Canada's present relief policy. It urges the need of leadership in respect of unemployment and relief to end the moral and social stagnation of the present situation. It says:
There is at present a most vital challenge to the statesmen and leaders of Canadian national life, which to our mind is paramount to all other problems, that of finding some solution to the unemployment problem with which is tied up the moral and social stagnation which it engenders. Everyone is agreed that continual dishing out of relief cannot ever solve the dilemma; it merely hastens the evil day when the national structure would crumble because the fibre is eaten away.
Happiness, contentment and national wellbeing come only by honest work and an adequate recompense giving a measure of security for the people. The course we are drifting along now is an unpractical one and a vicious one because it is destroying something which wont be built up so easily again.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for my overtime, and I trust that the government may give what the country is asking for, the action which they promised in 1935.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne, I am sorry to say, does not indicate any effective solution of the many difficulties that confront the people of Canada to-day. There is no solution offered for the many problems which have vexed our people now for many years, and many of which have increased in severity since the Liberal party have occupied the seats of authority. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) has stated that the present administration is a do-nothing government. With that I agree. But we must also remember that the government of which the hon. member himself was a member occupied the seats of authority in the years 1930 to

The Address-Mr. Landeryou
1935 and were defeated, in fact suffered the greatest defeat that party has ever experienced.
Reference has been made to the coming visit to Canada of Their Majesties King George VI and Queen Elizabeth. All classes of the Canadian people view with pleasure the coming visit. However, greater pleasure would be evidenced in many quarters if economic conditions which now obtain in Canada were not in such a chaotic state, if the widespread and needless suffering and misery which now abound in this country had been corrected by the present administration. In the speech from the throne we find the following words:
The government shared in the general sense of relief that the appalling disaster of war, which threatened Europe during the month of September last, was averted, and in the recognition which that crisis manifested of the widespread will of the peoples for peace. They are hopeful that the efforts now being made to find a solution for the specific differences which are causing friction will meet with success. They recognize, nevertheless, that time is required for these forces to work, and that the possibility of further tension in the meantime must be faced. In this situation, the government have considered that the uncertainties of the future, and the conditions of modern warfare, make it imperative that Canada's defences be materially strengthened.
Two years ago, the appropriations for defence were substantially increased, and a beginning made on a program of modernization to safeguard the country from the dangers of attack. The government intend to pursue this policy vigorously, and to propose to parliament that the program of defence should be further augmented, and that particular emphasis should be laid upon air defence.
Thus we find that the government recognizes the danger in the European situation and intends to take steps to preserve Canada's national integrity against attack. In so far as the danger of attack is concerned I am not greatly alarmed, for I cannot think of any nation in Africa, in Asia or in Europe which could consider at the present time or in years to come any successful invasion of this country; and I say this after considering the statement recently made by the President of the United States to the effect that that republic was prepared to come to the assistance of Canada in case of attack. However, in view of existing conditions I am not opposed to the government strengthening Canada's defences providing the money expended will be issued debt free. The last war created much hardship; many problems arose, and I believe that the method we used in financing that war was responsible for a great many of these problems. We must take the profits out of war. It has been estimated that it cost $25,000 for every soldier killed in the last war. Someone was making a profit out
of every body that lies on the fields of battle. It was blood-money. We are opposed to the method pursued during the last war of piling up debts which future generations are left to face.
The mad race for armaments has been going on in the world for many years. Billions of dollars have been spent. Tremendous wealth and energy have been expended. Germany, a country smaller in area than the province of Ontario, and with a population of over seventy millions of people, has spent billions of dollars. France, small in area, with a population of over forty million people, has spent billions of dollars on armaments besides providing for the needs of her people. Italy, also small in area, with a population of approximately fifty millions, has spent billions of dollars upon instruments of destruction. The same is true of England. Thus we find that in the four countries I have mentioned, where more than two hundred millions of people live, billions of dollars have been appropriated for the production of implements of war. How is it that Canada, having a large geographical area, with a population of approximately twelve million people, with more natural resources per capita than are possessed by any other people on earth, cannot maintain its institutions? How is it that our educational and health facilities are being undermined? How is it that municipal, provincial and federal governments are unable to finance the social and economic legislation which they feel is necessary? How is it that we are told that the deficits of the Canadian National Railways will bankrupt Canada? All this in spite of the fact that Canada is fifth among the great trading nations of the world? Something is radically wrong with our economic set-up. There is no good reason for the widespread suffering and want which exist in Canada, where we have only twelve million people, willing and anxious to provide from its tremendous natural resources all the commodities they may desire.
I wish to refer now to some questions by Mr. Hellmuth and some answers by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) as contained on page 10 of the report of the royal commission on the Bren machine gun contract. The question was asked by Mr. Hellmuth:
So that there has been no change in the actual policy of the government, or of the Minister of National Defence, that government ownership is the best and that the next is competition ?
The answer was:
Quite correct, provided you will give us the finances, the money.
The Address-Mr. Landeryou

Q. Yes; if you do not have money you cannot do anything?
A. Money is everything; when you are running the Department of National Defence you can t run it without money.
Q. I put it before you here, that the best plan is government ownership?
A. I thoroughly agree with you.
The minister said that there were two very definite schools of thought in the department and that he assumed all responsibility. One school, he said, was headed by the then chief of general staff and the other by the deputy minister, for both of whom he said he had equally great admiration.
The minister said that General Ashton (the then chief of the general staff) was very insistent upon the development of government arsenals and that the former chief of general staff, General McN aught on, evolved a very comprehensive scheme for Yalcartier which would include practically all the requirements of the Canadian forces.
That was considered after I went into the department and I found that the cost of it would be something between $30,000,000 and $35,000,000. With my meagre $25,000,000 or $30,000,000, what could I do with a scheme like that?
I heartily agree with the Minister of Defence that money is everything. You cannot do very much without money. But I would remind the government and particularly the Minister of Defence that in 1935 the Liberal party went to the people of Canada with the outstanding promise of monetary reform. They stated that control of money and credit should be restored to parliament and considered as its most sacred obligation. They further stated that money and credit would be issued to meet the industrial, the public and domestic need. That promise has not been fulfilled, in spite of the declaration by the Prime Minister that all the promises of the Liberal party have been carried out. We find now that the Minister of National Defence is unable to carry out the policies in which he and his advisers believe. Why? Because they are short of money. I have no hesitation in saying that many of the other ministers who sit on the treasury benches are faced with exactly the same problem. They find it impossible, on account of lack of money, to pursue many of the policies they and their advisers support.
Increased purchasing power is Canada's most urgent need at the present time. Municipal and provincial governments as well as the federal government are in need of more money. The consumers of the country are in need of more money to purchase commodities and services that can be-produced and rendered in Canada. When we advocate increased purchasing power for the Canadian people, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) at once sets up straw men and begins to knock them down. Others say that we are out to turn the printing presses loose and flood the country

with Bank of Canada bills. We have never advocated such a policy. All we say to the government is that they should have our monetary system reflect our collective ability to produce and render goods and services in Canada; that when there is idle labour and unused material, money should be issued so that that unused material and idle labour can be brought into production. We say, go thus far. Issue purchasing power so that the amount of money available in the hands of the people will be sufficient to equate the value of the goods and services that can be produced and rendered in Canada. In other words, make financially possible that which is already physically possible.
Before the election in 1935 the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said that in the next parliament a great battle would be fought with the money powers. Instead of battling with the money powers they battled with the provinces. They have battled with the provinces on many occasions. They have battled with the money powers against the provinces. They have even battled with one another. It is no wonder the premier of Ontario declares that he is no longer a Mackenzie King Liberal; no wonder the farmers of Saskatchewan advocate secession; no wonder the Liberal government of that province forwards a resolution to the federal government requesting them to carry out the promise with regard to monetary reform.
The policies pursued by this government are gradually undermining confederation and democracy in Canada. Ways and means can and must be found of correcting our economic ills without the surrender of any of our democratic rights, without centralizing authority in this government, without establishing a dictatorship, without making the provinces either politically or financially subservient. The democratic rights of our people can best be preserved by maintaining provincial autonomy.
The election slogan of the Liberal party in the 1935 campaign was "King or chaos." Unfortunately we got both. Where is the cooperation that was to exist between the federal government and the provinces? Among many things, the trade tariff and monetary policies pursued by this government have worked inimically to the best interests of many sections of Canada. The disabilities from which those sections are suffering must be corrected. I see no indication in the speech from the throne that the government intends to discuss these matters with the provinces apart from the possible discussion of unemployment. One would be led to believe, after listening to speeches made by members of the Liberal party, that all the loyalty in

The Address-Mr. Landeryou
Canada was wrapped up in the bosom of that party. Let me say, however, that Alberta and we who represent that province are as loyal to confederation as are any of those who now occupy treasury benches, and I am sure the same could be said of the other provinces and their representatives, no matter to which party they may belong. However, any slogan of "King and unity" to replace the "King or chaos" slogan of 1935 will not be accepted by the Canadian people unless definite action is taken to remove the many injustices from which they are suffering.
Reference has been made to the new trade agreement recently signed by Canada and the United States. We are in favour of world trade, but not of trade war. We believe that more attention should be paid to the development of Canada's home markets. Much could be done in the development of our coal, oil and sugar industries. In fact, I have read recently many editorials in the Halifax Herald depicting the terrible condition that exists in connection with the miners and fishermen of Nova Scotia. I visited the coal mining areas of Alberta and asked in one particular section what the problem was there. They said that it was simply a problem of unemployment and partial employment. They said that if an order could be secured for two million tons of coal their troubles would be over. We import from fifteen to seventeen million tons of coal every year. Why talk about blasting our way into foreign markets when we cannot secure our own?
Let me read from a pamphlet put out by L. R. Lipsett, K.C.. LL.D., O.B.E. Under the title, "National Coal Policy for Canada," the author writes:
Had the provinces of Ontario and Quebec during the past thirty years, taken a broad view of what was necessary for the prosperity of Canada as a whole, and had those provinces adapted themselves to using Canadian coal, much might have been done to redress the adverse trade balance, but eastern Canada blindly continued to import millions of tons of American coal, for the sake of immediate sayings in expense, regardless of the fact that this was bound to make other provinces, sooner or later, unable to pay for the goods they manufactured.
Results, apparent to everyone to-day, might well have been foreseen for a number of years past, had a longer view been taken by the eastern manufacturing and financial interests, by the Canadian railways, and by the various governments from time to time in power.
The drain on nation finances.
The second outstanding fact which emerged from a study of the problem from the national standpoint, is the enormous annual drain on Canadian resources necessary to pay for importations of American coal. In the coal statistics for Canada (Coal Statistics for Canada, 1936. Page 18.), published by the dominion bureau of statistics, it is stated that
about $450,000,000 were sent out of Canada during the last ten years for imported coal, practically all of which was sent to the United States of America. This was the figure paid to the American mine owners for coal, and when the railway freights from the American mines to the Canadian border are added, the money sent out of the country during these ten years, would far exceed $500,000,000, or a sum of over $50,000,000 each year.
Consider for one moment what this sum, it it had been kept at home, would have meant to Canada, and the effect it would have had on the balance of trade as between Canada and the outside world. Consider also the effect, during these past ten years, of the creation within Canada of this $50,000,000 of new wealth each year, and its contribution to the wellbeing of the country, and to the problem of unemployment, vdiich has been so acute during most of the period.
If one assumes that $5 per day would represent an average day's wage, then this $50,000,000 annually sent out of Canada would represent approximately 10,000,000 days work each year, or enough to give employment to well over
40,000	unemployed men for about eight months each year.
Direct prosperity would certainly accrue to the Eastern manufacturers and workers who would receive substantial orders, not now forthcoming, as a result of the enormously increased buying power of the workers and operators in the coal producing areas of Canada, and of the railways and railway workers, who would benefit by its transportation.
I ask the government to consider passing much needed social legislation. If they would reduce the age for qualification for the old age pension to sixty, this would provide an opportunity for employment for thousands of young men now tramping the highways and byways of this country in search of work. If they would provide pensions to widows of ex-service men who saw service in actual theatres of war, they would also be helping a very worthy class. From the letters I have received from many of these widows, I know how difficult it is for them to establish the fact that the death of their husbands could be attributed to war causes. I should like to read a letter from the Canadian Soldier Non-Pensioned Widows' Association:
We the Canadian soldier non-pensioned widows request you to give your consideration to the following:
First the sacred promise made by Canada's War Prime Minister-The Right Honourable R. L. Borden-"That, Canadians we are proud of you, you can rest assured that you and your kin will never suffer, Canada owes that to you for the great honour you have brought to our great dominion."
Since the great war ended many of our Canadian heroes returned, but through their great sacrifices have gone to an early grave, leaving their dependents in unfortunate circumstances over which they had no control, have been forced to exist upon unemployed relief. As the widows of pensioners are receiving a full pension we request that as our loss is equal to theirs that we also be fully pensioned.
The Address-Mr. Landeryou

We gave our consent for our husbands to give their all for our glorious empire, that it would he maintained for the honour, glory and benefit of civilized Christianity-we therefore ask that the War Prime Minister's promises be upheld.
I also have received a request from the city of Calgary that this government pass legislation to provide financial assistance to expectant mothers during the period of their confinement. The letter states:
The special health committee of the council of the city of Calgary, in meeting recently, gave consideration to a report from the city's medical officer of health, Dr. Hill, wherein it was stated that infant mortality in the city of Calgary, as elsewhere in the Dominion of Canada, was overly heavy due to the fact that expectant mothers were not being given any financial assistance either by the dominion, provincial or municipal governments. Dr. Hill believed, and so stated in his report, that the situation in this regard could be considerably improved upon if an expectant mother was assured some financial assistance during the period of her confinement.
I should like the government also to consider the advisability of reducing the age at which the blind may qualify for pension from forty to twenty-one years. That has been done in New Zealand.
Just here I should like to refer to a statement made by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), as follows:
This statement is proven by what has occurred in New Zealand, where a government with philosophy and ideals similar to those which we advocate has been able since 1935 to assist the people of that country to solve problems which, according to the speech from the throne now before us, seem insoluble.
I thoroughly enjoyed the address of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, but I cannot agree when he attempts to say that the ideals and principles of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation are being implemented in New Zealand, or that the government of that country is attempting to translate the ideals of his party into reality there. I have read many speeches delivered by the Prime Minister of New Zealand and his colleagues, and in them I find no reference whatever to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation or to socialism. I should like to read the statement made by the Prime Minister of New Zealand, Hon. M. J. Savage, when he was questioned as to his connection with the social credit organization:
The Prime Minister (Hon. M. J. Savage) said the leader of the opposition had accused the government of having made arrangements with the Douglas credit organizations. Now, what were the Douglas credit organizations trying to do? They were trying to get for the people the things that the people were capable of producing. Well, who had a better right to them than the people themselves? There was any amount of room for difference of

opinion about this; that, unless the buying power of the people was enough to equate the value of their production they would never get out of the mudhole which the last government created for the country. Unless the buying power of the people increased with the increasing production, what was the use of increasing production?
They had the right to govern in the financial sphere; and everything they did in that sphere *was based on the public credit. Had not the time come for basing their money system on the goods they produced and the services they rendered to each other?
Then, from the report of another speech made before eight thousand people at the King Edward barracks, Auckland, I quote;
The Prime Minister said that unless the government of a country controlled the credit of the country it could not control anything else.
"I don't suggest that this means socialization. ... I am not prepared to predict what will happen to the money system in this or any other country at any long period ahead, but I do believe that there can be no freedom unless the mass of the people have freedom to buy, and that is economic freedom. Without economic freedom no nation can ever be free." The clear objective of the labour party was to make money the servant of man instead of the master.
So I believe the government of New Zealand is attempting to implement the principles and ideals for which the social credit party of this country stands. I should like to refer also to a statement by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), appearing at page 60 of Hansard for January 16, 1939:
Men will not put out their money to invest in the different industries. They are withdrawing their capital from industry. Ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), who is sitting here to-night, how much of the investment of capital to-day is going into government securities at a low rate of interest in comparison with what took place in former years.
Then he went further:
Labour and capital are both essential to production, and whatever paralyzes one paralyzes the other in the matter of effective production.
There are many factors that enter into this industrial paralysis. I do not believe it is as simple as saying that when capital is paralyzed, labour is idle and industry slumps. I believe that if the consumers of this country had more money, that money would be spent on goods and the wheels of industry would turn once more. The reason for industrial paralysis is not any fear of something external; it is the definite knowledge in the minds of those who control capital that if they were to invest their money in creating more products of industry, the people would be unable to pay for them; for to-day, as for many years past, we find the great production of Canadian industry

The Address-Mr. Fleming
being disposed of on the instalment plan, fifty cents or a dollar down and a dollar when you catch me. If we have to mortgage the future in order to purchase these goods to-day; if we have to allow these loan shark companies to loan millions and millions of dollars to the consumers in order to complete the purchase of goods bought on the instalment plan, it should be apparent to all that the only thing this country needs is more purchasing power. Municipal, provincial and federal governments require it just as much as the consumers require it. I plead with the government to take definite steps to deal with Canada's social and economic problems, so that a greater measure of peace, happiness and prosperity may be made available to all.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks this afternoon I should like to offer my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Matthews) and seconder (Mr. Chevrier) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
During the parliamentary recess the right hon. leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King) again demonstrated to the Canadian people that he is one of our greatest statesmen. His handling of the international crisis through which we passed deserves the approbation and gratitude of the entire nation. His conception of the Canadian angle of the problem was dominated by past pronouncements made in this house and to the Canadian electorate; and while jingoistic newspaper writers from coast to coast thundered against him, he remained steadfast to those pronouncements and never once made a false move or issued an unconsidered statement.
We also have reason, Mr. Speaker, to be proud of the calibre of the men in the public life of this country. May I congratulate the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) upon his election to that high office and also upon gaining a seat in the House of Commons. He took the stand of a statesman and followed the best of British traditions when, in our hour of greatest peril, he offered no criticism of the government, but said that he was ready to stand by and aid in any emergency. That was the stand of a statesman and a soldier, and one which has enhanced his reputation in the hearts and minds of many Canadians. Such chivalry is characteristic of only one race, the Irish, to which he belongs.
Another event of extraordinary interest has occurred in the interval since parliament prorogued. Their Gracious Majesties the King and Queen have agreed to visit these shores, the first reigning monarchs ever to visit a dominion. We are deeply honoured and
jubilant. Their visit will do much, if such were needed, to reaffirm our belief in the soundness of our political alliances. Their visit to the United States we may be confident will also do much toward cementing the friendly feeling which exists between the empire and the great democracy to the south of us, whose long and mutual accord and respect we deeply value, and of which we are so justly proud. No words of greater import were ever uttered in human history than when last summer at the opening of an international bridge, in the presence of the king's representatives and in the presence of the Prime Minister of Canada and responsible ministers of the crown, the President of the United States said that if Canada were ever attacked the United States would not stand idly by.
The visit of their majesties will give us an opportunity of showing them our loyalty and devotion to their persons. It has been my fond hope that my constituency might have had an opportunity of giving such a demonstration. While I realize that their majesties' time is limited, I thought it would have been a nice gesture on their part if they could have visited the largest German and Icelandic settlements in Canada. Many of my constituents come from the Munich area in Germany, where Mr. Hitler and Mr. Chamberlain signed the famous peace pact to keep peace in our time. The constituency of Humboldt would have given the king and queen a reception which might in other places have been surpassed in grandeur and volume but nowhere else in sincerity.
In the interval between the prorogation of the last session and the opening of the present one we have become parties to the signing of one of the greatest trade pacts ever negotiated in history. From a long term point of view I cannot help but believe that it will have tremendous beneficial effects, both economically and politically. But Mr. Speaker, as I review the accomplishments of the present government and of our own political term in office, and as I have listened attentively to the proposals in the speech from the throne, I begin to wonder how long it will be before the government will be willing to face fairly the fundamental issues, instead of permitting itself to be occupied merely with details of administration.
In my view we have been following the proper path externally. Faced with high tariff barriers throughout the world we have negotiated trade treaties with nations who have wished to trade with us. We did not simply sit back and trade among ourselves, an attitude which would have been disastrous
The Address-Mr. Fleming
