to our position as the fifth trading nation of the world. In our political relations with other nations at least we have made no serious errors.
Of course there is the question whether or not we are putting our full weight behind our empire defence scheme. But generally speaking, under all circumstances, I think we have done perhaps considerably better than could be expected. On the other hand, internally, we seem to be floundering around, not that we have made so many mistakes. Someone will say, "Well, if you are speaking of social reform, the answer is that we cannot do anything until the federal government has more power." Any practical man will say, "Do it anyway"-and I am glad to find in the speech from the throne that this is the attitude of the present administration when it says:
My ministers recognize that the plight of those who are still unemployed cannot await necessary constitutional amendments, nor the summoning of any conference. They are prepared therefore, notwithstanding constitutional impediments to effective action, to join with the provinces in a further determined effort to meet the immediate situation.
Once again I think the Prime Minister is on the right track, but progress along that track seems painfully slow. There is no sense in passing laws, if they are to remain inoperative. There is no use in passing laws if they are to be thrown out by the courts. As I hear hon. members opposite and people throughout the country criticizing royal commissions, I often wonder why members of the House of Commons and members of the Senate could not occupy positions on those commissions just as well as impractical university professors and editorial writers on the newspapers. In every session, after the opening days, the Senate adjourns. As a matter of fact it has just adjourned for about a month. In that chamber there are men occupying high positions in the state, men who are privy councillors of the empire, men who stand high in the business, financial and economic world. Why could we not place them on commissions, instead of appointing royal commissioners? In that regard I agree with some hon. members opposite when they say that every time we face a knotty problem we appoint a royal commission-and then the government does what it wanted to do anyway. The only thing I can ever say for a royal commission is that the government has a splendid goat at its disposal, and if the recommendations of the commission do not work out satisfactorily it can be blamed.
I am not complaining that we are not doing good. My complaint is that we are not

doing enough good, or at least not getting round to it fast enough. That is the attitude of the people in my constituency. The British North America Act should and could have been amended long ago, but I hold the suspicion that in the minds of some members of t'he government and many members of the house there lurks this thought: If you amend the British North America Act, there goes the best alibi you ever had in your life. I say this: If we do not amend it, we shall drift into a mess for which we shall never be able to find an alibi.
In what manner did the speech from the throne convey to us the fact that we are facing a critical, if not a crucial, period in the history of Canada and the world at large? We came through one world crisis, and we have no assurance that we shall not have to face another one in the near future. The speech from the throne contains many first-class suggestions, but why do we dislike to face realities? Why do we struggle so hard, to preserve the impression that we are still dealing with the "common round"; that the world around us is not changing, that the affairs of men move smoothly, and that we can be smugly complacent about the situation? National and world economy has become a hopeless tangle. Production for need has become all mixed up with exploitation for profit. In Canada we see poverty and desperation. When we have nearly a million people on relief and the granaries are filled with wheat, do we take the wheat and put men to work making bread for those who have none? No; we plunge the country farther into debt by borrowing money to get the bread. Goods are sacrificed for profit not only in this country but in others. Brazil dumps coffee into the ocean; California throws oranges on the dump heap; British Columbia allows her apples to rot in the orchards; the United States deliberately slaughters her hogs. While all this is happening, in my constituency there are children who have grown from babies and have never seen an apple or even an orange. There are hundreds and hundreds of families who for years have used roasted barley as a substitute for coffee-and yet we stick to this worldwide valorization.
What do we contribute to the problem? Before the house there are bills and still more bills, talk and still more talk, none of which touches the vital problems with which we are concerned. In my opinion no harm and perhaps a considerable amount of good would be done if, during an entire session, we threw every petty problem into the future and tried

The Address-Mr. Fleming
to work out a remedy for the defects of our political, social and economic organization. If that course did nothing else, at least it would permit us to see clearly the difficulties which confront us.
It is all too easy to think, in terms of ourselves and our supporters, of the problems of the moment. In other words, we think of those matters which, to the dominion as a whole, are only small. If we could solve the big problems, most of the small ones would never arise. If we do not solve the big problems, our power to solve them may be taken away from us. Those are neither idle words nor a threat, but a statement of grim reality.
Undoubtedly the biggest problem of all is the present plight of our people. "The people keep the government, but the government does not keep the people." By this I do not mean that we should keep the people on relief. The people ask for an opportunity to earn a living, and we give them charity. They do not want it; we do not want it, and the country cannot stand it forever.
Mr. L. T. Hobhouse, in his book on Liberalism, British Liberalism-and I consider that the excerpt I am going to give is equally applicable to-day to Canadian Liberalism- says:
The right to work and the right to a living wage are just as valid as the rights of person or property. They are integral conditions of a good social order. A society in which a single honest man of normal capacity is definitely unable to find the means of maintaining himself by useful work is to that extent suffering from malorganization. There is somewhere a defect in the social system, a hitch in the economic machine. Now, the individual workman cannot put the machine straight. He is the last person to have any say in the control of the market. It is not his fault that there is overproduction in his industry, or if new and cheaper processes have been introduced which makes his particular skill-a drug on the market. He does not direct or regulate industry. He is not responsible for its ups and downs. But he has to pay for them. That ' is why it is not charity but justice for which he is asking.
That, Mr. Speaker, to me is Liberalism.
The individual cannot right conditions by himself, and so he looks to the government to do it. What is the government's answer? Direct relief cannot remain indefinitely the answer. We should do away with relief as soon as possible. I do not believe that we should let the people starve. But there seems to be a conception that because we are keeping the unemployed, we are relieved of all obligation to help them to secure employment.
But what have we done about our basic obligation as a state, which is to secure conditions under which mind and character may
best develop by themselves? It is to me ridiculous, it is stupid, it is asinine that crops should be ploughed under, that fish should be thrown back into the sea, that hogs should be slaughtered, when so many people are starving or living barely above the subsistence level. Do we need people to work, to produce and feed them? They are more than available. We are supporting them in idleness. Do we need land and resources with which to produce? Millions of fertile acres are lying idle for the plough of the husbandman, waiting for their riches to be turned into gold. Idle men and idle acres do not add up to prosperity. And, Mr. Speaker, agriculture, our basic industry, lies crushed and bleeding from a thousand wounds. The leader of the Liberal party, now Prime Minister of this country, on that eventful night of October 14, 1935, issued the following statement to the Canadian people:
We take up at once, as our supreme task, the endeavour to end poverty in the midst of plenty, starvation and unnecessary suffering in a land of abundance, discontent and distress in a country more blessed by Providence than any other on the face of the globe, and to gain for individual lives, and for the nation as a whole, that "health and peace and sweet content" which is the rightful heritage of all.
A back-to-the-land movement will not solve that problem because hundreds and hundreds of our experienced farmers on the plains of Saskatchewan and of western Canada are starving. The problem goes deeper, much deeper, than that.
One step that will have to be taken is to provide more money for productive purposes, for individual enterprise, and coincident with that there must be a better price to the primary producer for his products. If fewer people are to get more and more of the money, through a system which permits excessive profits to the few, then we can continue to expect more and more people with less and less money; and when less becomes nothing, the state has to support them.
For a long time I have been a believer in sound money, as some people call it. For a long time I have worshipped at the shrine of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), when he was Premier of Saskatchewan and while he has been Minister of Finance here. But, Mr. Speaker, the more I have read and the more I have studied the solutions that have been offered by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), and other monetary reformers, the more convinced and persuaded I have become that we must get more money into circulation, even though we have to use methods of inflation. I do not think we need to be afraid of inflation,
The Address-Mr. Fleming

but we have been afraid of it ever since it was tried in the old post-war days in Germany. But in Germany they have inflation to-day, and Germany is apparently one of the most prosperous countries in the world. What I cannot understand is this:	If there
were a war to-morrow we would get all the money we wanted. It seems to me that you can get all you want for destruction, but as little as can be spared for construction.
As to the feverish armament race that is now going on in the world, on the one hand I can see the necessity for the empire rearming, but on the other I cannot help being suspicious about it. Of course, if we are not armed, we are certainly a temptation to ruthless aggressors, and surely our September scare must have indicated how rapidly we could all be drawn into the whirlpool before we knew anything about-what was happening. In a madly rearming world, can we afford to remain blissfully insecure, while greedy nations eye our undeveloped wealth as one of the richest prizes on earth? Yet, no matter what we do in the way of armaments, I think we should let the world know we are certainly on the side of democracy, justice and peace.
But we cannot shirk much longer our responsibilities as part of the empire. The motherland is not going to force us into doing our part, but she has made known her desire that she would like the dominion to be able to look after its own defence. On the other hand, the world situation is far from hopeless. There have always been divergent opinions in the world. If. those who are in the right have the intelligence, the courage and the morale of their convictions, they will win through. It is not inconceivable that the totalitarian states and the democracies can live and work together in peace. It is not any more for us to say that Germany should have this or that type of government than it is for Germany to say that democracies should give up their priceless privilege of freedom. Surely we who live in the democracies should count our blessings. But we cannot talk too enthusiastically about the virtues of democracy until we prove that democracy has those virtues. We would be better advised to spend less time in criticizing the Hitler regime and more time in bolstering up our own weaknesses. The best criticism anyone can give of a dictatorship is a perfectly functioning democracy.
Our freedom was hard won. Our forefathers paid for it in blood and tears. Are we to be unworthy of that heritage? Are we to let the world slip back into the dark night of oblivion because of our ineompet-

ency, because of our neglect, because of our failure to see our problems and to see them whole? Or shall we keep the beacon light of democracy burning to light the rest of the world which has taken the by-path back on the road to freedom?
Democracy is not perfect. It is as fallible as the people who compose it. In the democratic state, though the good generally prevails because the majority must be pleased, special or malignant groups cannot thrive for long, as larger groups will generally turn them out of power. On the other hand, it is true that the majority does not always realize its power, or even that it is being exploited. That is when an intelligent leadership is so desirable and necessary.
Conditions in most parts of western Canada this year, Mr. Speaker, have been, to say the least, desperate. It is a combination of poor wheat markets over a period of years, and no wheat or anything else to sell because of drought, grasshoppers and rust. Fortunately this year those who were lucky enough to have rust-resistant wheat had some grain to sell. The government fixed a price of eighty cents a bushel. This was done, I trust, after mature thought by the government, and not as the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) said, as the result of a by-election in the constituency of Humboldt. I do not know what we should have done if the government had not set a price for wheat. I believe a panic would have resulted in western Canada.
We all realize that the self-sufficiency policy of most countries in the last decade has led to a curtailment of our markets and to an increase in the production of wheat. But it sometimes seems to me as if the people of eastern Canada, and even Premier Hepburn and Premier Duplessis, wanted to add a few frills of their own and to turn the world's great wheat basket into a wastebasket.
The wheat farmer mostly competes in the open market to sell his products. But in order to produce he must buy his implements in a protected market, and we find right now that the western farmers and many of my constituents are not so much interested in the price they receive for their wheat as in getting the commodities which they use reduced in price. As to wheat this year, with the fixed price, the concession that we have made in the British market will not alter the selection greatly. What effect the six cent preference we enjoyed had on the actual market was sometimes disputed; but the selection would be vastly altered if we did not have that fixed price for wheat. So it further indicates to the government the necessity of retaining it over a period of years.

The Address-Mr. Fleming
In giving up the British preference, what compensation has the west received? We were hoping that we could see a fairly certain gleam that there would be a reduction in the price of our tools of production or in our cost of living. Two things are of main importance to the western farmer, farm implements and gasoline. Gasoline was not mentioned in the trade treaty; and there is no lowering of the duty on United States implements coming into Canada. This may help the Canadian manufacturer; I do not know; but it certainly will not have any effect in cutting down the price of farm implements. In fact, I am not emphasizing the point because experience has shown us that even if the duty is cut, it does not succeed in lowering the price of farm implements to any great extent, if at all. When you take the duty off the manufacturing companies raise the price anyway. Shortly before the trade agreement was made public, the implement companies turned round and lowered the price. This was perhaps not so much related to what the tariff will be, as to the fact that there was not the tariff to bear it. After the duty was cut in 1935, the price of farm implements actually increased.
I have no hesitation in saying that the price of gasoline and the price of farm implements are out of all proportion and are far too high. Every investigation, including our own and the inquiry in the United States into the price of farm implements, has sustained that fact. The reason that reductions in duty will do little to force the price down is that there is a combination which acts as an international monopoly.
In the report last summer of the federal trade commission upon its investigation into the agricultural implement and machine industry in the United States, this statement is made:	.
The effect on prices of this concentration of production is such that, with respect to the most important farm implements, the prices established by the leading manufacturers, especially International Harvester Co. and Deere & Co., constitute, in so far as the machines are of closely similar character, the price level which all manufacturers observe.
The small companies generally cannot sell their products for more than the established prices of widely accepted similar products of the large companies; nor do they feel free to sell for less than the price leaders for fear of starting a price war in which their large and financially stronger rivals would have all the advantage.
Lest their prices be out of line, it is the practice among lesser manufacturers to await the announcement of prices by the leading companies at the beginning of each season before announcing their own. Similarly, the price leadership of the large companies is followed
in price changes made during selling seasons. In general, any price reductions are restricted to implements or machines for which the leaders of the industry have announced reductions.
In summarizing the effect of concentration on prices, the trade commissioner's report states:
It does not take either imagination or insight to perceive that the same sort of thing obtains in Canada, where the market is dominated by subsidiaries of the American companies.
Not only do the rich get richer and the poor poorer, but it seems in these days as though the small corporation and the small business man have no chance at all. In the meantime the consuming public suffers. Let me quote again from the federal trade commission's report on farm implements. They say:
Domination of the farm implement and machinery industry by a few leading manufacturers has resulted in the maintenance of the prices of their products at levels far higher than those of farm products and of the prices of other manufactured products of somewhat comparable material and labour. There was a more or less general decline in the prices of farm machinery from 1929 through the years of severest industrial depression. 1932 and 1933. However, this decline was slight in comparison with the decline in the farm prices of the principal farm products.
What can be done? Government fixing of a maximum price level would not, I think, be advisable because either labour or the quality of the goods would suffer. Yet if some way cannot soon be found to make the implement manufacturers toe the line, the government will have to set up manufacturing plants under the control of the government; or if we do. not want to do that, we shall have to make arrangements with some other countries, like Germany, and get them to manufacture our implements and bring them into this country, because the farmers of western Canada absolutely cannot go on as they are doing for another period of years; conditions are going from bad to worse.
Something also should be done about the price of gasoline. It would not surprise me one bit, if we had an investigation into the price of gasoline, that we should find that the same international monopoly exists as is to be found in connection with the price of farm implements. Whatever it is that is sustaining the price out of all proportion to prices of primary products, the government should not wait until next year but should certainly take some steps this year to eliminate this condition.
No problem in this country demands so much immediate attention as the welfare of the primary producer, particularly the farmer. If the farmer is prosperous, never fear but that
The Address-Mr. Fleming

the city will be prosperous. One part of the problem is for the farmer to obtain a reasonable price for his products. Another part is that he should not have to pay an unreasonable price for other goods. To-day he is caught between the scissors. He is cut to the bone on the price paid to him for his products, and at the same time the pittance he receives for his goods is cut deeply by the price of the tools of production and the charge for the amenities of living.
No trade treaty ever designed could satisfy everybody. It is impossible at one and the same time to please the producer and the consumer. But the general object of such a treaty should be for instance, to permit Canada to sell in the United States goods which the United States is unable to produce as efficiently or in sufficient quantities, and to permit the United States to come to Canada with goods which we cannot produce efficiently here. If there is to be some sacrifice, it should be in the artificial industries. I would not look with favour upon destroying industry. I should be seriously concerned if for one moment I thought that by taking off the tariff we should be destroying the factories in the riding of the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario (Mr. Fraser); but that consequence is always a debatable point. But if the factories where the hon. member for Northumberland lives, are making exorbitant profits in a protected market, and at the same time bleeding to death another part of our economy, not only do 1 fail to see the value of such protection, but I think it is vicious.
There are a number of items omitted frorr. the trade treaty which I should have likeo to see included. Yet the real test of the treaty, and only time will tell, is, will it result in a freer flow of goods between this country and the United States? For England we are a convenient factory to have in case of war, but she too can make better arrangements with her neighbours. Of course we do not wish to lose the British market, and I do not think we shall. But the United States is our natural market. Sometimes I think it would have been much better for us from the first if we had been trading from north to south in place of from east to west; if instead of travelling along a four thousand mile line we could have traded over a few hundred miles between the north and the south.
Definitely, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the treaty is a step in the right direction. It has lowered duties on a broad front, and it is designed to exchange goods. That is what we need if we are ever to get back to prosperity. It also links us with the two great trad-

ing nations of the earth. It has long been my view that belligerent dictators would be most vulnerable to an economic union of the democratic states. Democracy is worth fighting for, but we do not have to go around with a chip on our shoulder talking about the totalitarian state. Democracy is such a magnificent ideal, it would be a shame to let it perish from the face of the earth because of our incompetence or because we were unable to mould it to our purpose. If we could make this land and the system under which we live so desirable that the peoples of all countries would wish to come and live here, never fear, it would not be long before other countries would accept our system of government. No man can teach an entire nation for long. The people in Germany turned from democracy, just as the people in Canada will turn from democracy if the government of Canada and of the other democratic nations will not try to make the people happy and contented, but rather hold them down as economic slaves. In the name of the people of Canada, in the name of people with more ability than I have, I appeal to this house to do something for the starving inhabitants, and for the farmers, of western Canada.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Matthews) and the seconder (Mr. Chevrier) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am not an old member of the house and therefore I am not a critic, but I think those speeches were very fine indeed.
Before proceeding to the matter of the speech from the throne, I should like to say a word about the opening of parliament and the delivery of the speech in the senate chamber. This may be regarded as a secondary matter, but I think it needs to be said by someone.
Each year the opening of parliament is a much anticipated event. We might even say it is the outstanding event of the year, because parliament has the power to add to or take away from the welfare of eleven and a half million Canadian people. From all parts of Canada come the commoners, members of the senate, their families and friends, business men and various people representing all phases of Canadian life. The focus of this

The Address-Mr. Marsh
interest is the speech from the throne. Seated in the senate chamber, in the galleries, back in the foyer and thronging the corridors are representative Canadian people, waiting, hushed with expectancy. The speech begins, continues and ends, and except for those people within a radius of perhaps twenty feet of the speaker the one hour message is not heard.
It is far from my intention to criticize the speaker. His Excellency the Governor General, the representative of the king; but I do think the senate chamber, which at best is a difficult place in which to hear or be heard, should be equipped with an amplifier, which I believe could be installed very easily, in order that those who have come so far, for such an important event, might hear the speech from the throne rather than read it in the morning paper over a cup of coffee. As I was standing at the back of the senate chamber I was considerably embarrassed by the conversation and noise going on about me; yet I could not criticize those who were chatting, because I knew they could not hear. I submit that all the dignity of parliament and British traditions, each of which has a meaning to us in Canada to-day, requires that the speech from the throne be heard as it comes from the cultured lips of the governor general. In fact, I would go further and suggest that hundreds of thousands of loyal Canadians would like to hear the speech from the throne over the air. I am sure the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation would allow that.
I have listened to the excellent speeches on the address that have been made so far. We have heard from hon. members from the east, from the west, from the north and from the south, and I think there is no doubt that this parliament is problem conscious. We know the problems that beset our country today, but I would point out that we knew those problems last year, the year before and the year before that; yet we have not gone very far towards solving them. It is very seldom that I find myself able to agree with the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more), but he asked a very pertinent question. It was this: Does the government know what to do? The next question was:	If
the government knows what to do, will it do it? The next was:	Has the government
power? If the government has power, will it exercise that power?
From the press, from the pulpit, from newspapers throughout Canada and in private conversation with thinking men and women we have heard these questions asked:	Has
democracy failed? Has the government failed? Has community life failed? Has the family failed? Has the individual failed? Has the church failed? All these questions have been asked, and they have been answered by various people in various ways. I should like to take those questions now, put them all together, and unhesitatingly answer yes to all. Having done that, we can get ahead with the serious business of government.
There are some problems, Mr. Speaker, that are sapping at the very blood stream of Canadian life to-day. They are problems that are serious, and in this year of our Lord 1939, at this session of parliament, it is our job to do something about them. Therefore I say to the government-because we are in opposition here; we are handcuffed, tied hand and foot-"Give us legislation, and we will not obstruct it. Give us some policies and if they are any good we will not delay them. We will do our very best to augment, to push through, to pass any bills that are based on sound policy." But may we not flounder again as we have floundered during the past three years?
It is quite fresh in the memory of hon. members that last year we sat for almost six months. We wore the seats out of our trousers, while the man on the street was wearing the soles off his shoes hunting the job that it was our duty to create for him. We waited for the budget. The business men of Canada, the manufacturers and merchandisers, cannot buy; they cannot plan; they cannot budget until the financial statement of the government is brought down. We waited through February and March and April and May. I think it was June 16 when the budget was finally brought down for consideration in this house. In the meantime what was happening? In the city of Hamilton, where I live, there was very little smoke coming out of the chimneys, and there were very few wheels turning in our factories. There were men and women walking the streets of our city, while other men and women were working two or three days a week, getting very slim pay envelopes and depending partly upon relief.
What can we point to with pride in the work of last session? I should like to be fair; I should like to give credit where credit is due. There was a little housing; yes. Good. There was the removal of the sales tax on gopher poison, heavy harness and a few building materials. Good. The farmer buys heavy harness once every seven years, but at least it is a start. Then there was the

The Address-Mr. Marsh

removal of the sales tax on material for the making of fishermen's nets. Wis there anything else? Was there anything about unemployment insurance? No. Was there a reduction in taxation? No. Was there closer harmony between the provinces? No. Was there greater economy in spending? No. Was there any increased revenue from the customs tariff? No. Were there increased exports? No. Decreased exports? Yes.
Then, Mr. Speaker, after several months had gone by, we came to the bill to assist municipalities to relieve unemployment by making available to them $30,000,000 at two per cent. When this legislation was enunciated I was quite enthusiastic about it; but when we went into the provisions of the bill, we were sobered with the realization that the number of self-liquidating projects was extremely limited. Then we found that the bill could not come into operation until the provincial legislatures met, and at that time they had all prorogued for the summer. So it was necessary for them to be called together before the municipalities could take advantage of that act. How successful has that legislation been? How much of this $30,000,000 has been made available to the municipalities? I speak subject to correction; but my information is that out of the $30,000,000 only $2,900,000 has been made available to the municipalities of this country, with nothing being spent in the province of Quebec or the province of Ontario. That is a ten per cent success as far as this legislation is concerned. A business man would have very great difficulty in operating his business if, in any policy, he had only ten per cent of success and ninety per cent of failure.
1 should like to place on Hansard a news item from the Toronto Daily Star, under date of January 17, 1939:
Premier Hepburn's refusal to have Ontario guarantee low cost dominion loans for self-liquidating public works has tied up thirty-three Ontario municipalities. They wished to share the $30,000,000 made available by Ottawa last year, for such works as electric light, sewer and water systems.
The two per cent money was available if the loan was guaranteed by the province. Quebec and Ontario refused. In the other seven provinces loans aggregating $2,900,000 were made.
Ontario's attitude halted Toronto efforts to secure aid for its large sewage disposal scheme, but thirty-three other municipalities did make applications which are pigeonholed until the provincial guarantee is forthcoming. The applications are:
Owen Sound, city hall; Pelee township, draining system; Morrisburg, school; London, sewerage system; Burlington, water scheme; Kirkland Lake and Port Arthur, water and drainage systems; St. Thomas, nurses' home; Geraldton, water and sewerage systems; Hawkesbury, 
school hall and rink; Gravenhurst, sewerage Bystems; Western Ferris township, water system; Bowmanville. waterworks; West Lome, waterworks; Dymont township, sewerage; New Toronto, sewerage; Blind River, water and sewerage system; Hamilton, water mains; Larder Lake, water and sewerage; Etobicoke, sewerage; Harrow, town hall; Arnprior, electric light plant; Sault Ste. Marie, public market; Timmins, water and sewerage; Oshawa, city hall; Peel, school; Elmira, school; York township, electric plant; Delaware, school.
East York and North Bay were other municipalities which sought loans for various purposes.
I believe enough has been said respecting the self-liquidating project's measure for the municipalities.
On Monday last the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in impassioned language pointed out the cares of his office and the multiplicity of duties which were, his as Prime Minister of the country. I honour him in his position and I honour him because of his consciousness of his cares. But I feel myself called upon to say that he grossly overrates the impact which we in Canada have to make on world conditions. I believe that he grossly over-values the importance of Canada in world affairs, and that not one of his duties as Minister for External Affairs is as important as hand-to-hand contact and eye-to-eye conversation with the man on the street, his family, his sickness, his security, his job. The Prime Minister of Canada is out of touch with the common, ordinary man, and, if so, he is out of touch with Canada, because it is made up of common, ordinary men.
What is the greatest contribution we in this country can make to the world? What contribution can we make to world sanity and world business? What is the greatest contribution we can make to that highest of all pinnacles to be reached by human achievement-world peace? It is this, that we clean up our own door-step and solve our own problems. Do that, and we shall have made the finest contribution we could make to the British empire and the world at large.
I was much impressed with the speech made by our beloved leader (Mr. Manion). He pointed out that Great Britain has solved much of her difficulty through taxation-by collecting three times as much per capita, through customs and tariff charges, as we do in Canada. And yet under the trade treaty which was signed recently-and I shall have more to say about it at a later time-this government is prepared joyfully to lose a three per cent excise tax, which brings in about $18,000,000. Nevertheless it is content to continue to saddle the Canadian people with a sales tax which hits at the very root of the

The Address-Mr. Marsh
necessities of life, and which comes out of the pocket of the man who has to buy sugar, flour, shoes and those commodities he needs for his home and his work. We still have the sales tax; we still have the cheque tax; we still have the sugar tax. The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) brought it out very clearly, that in 1936 we collected $372,-
000.000 in taxation from the Canadian people, whereas in 1938 we collected $516,000,000 and, as he has said, the job is gone. I wonder how long a business man would stay in business if he practised the same methods our government has been practising for the last three years? With decreased revenues, would not a cutting down of expenditures seem to be a solution to the problem? Why should we spend money we do not have to spend?
Perhaps it may be urged that trade is the answer. A few days ago the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen pointed out in the senate that last year we exported $200,000,000 worth less of products and imported $90,000,000 less than we did in 1937. Now that we have opened our market to 120,000,000 people, what is going to become of our industry? It seems to me that in view of diminishing revenues there is only one way out, and that is to spend less money.
The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) never misses an opportunity to speak about his native county and, following his example, I should like to say a word about Hamilton. A few years ago in that city we were faced with bankruptcy. Our bonds were no good; our credit was not good. The mayor of Hamilton took it upon his shoulders to adopt a pay-as-you-go policy. It was his thought that if he took a dollar from the taxpayer of Hamilton, spent only ninety cents of it and put away the other ten cents to pay off our debt, conditions would greatly improve. Mr. Speaker, I am a very fortunate man; I have five children. As yet I have no grandchildren, but perhaps, being an optimist, I shall have. What right have I to spend a dollar that belongs to my children? What right have I to spend a dollar that belongs to the unborn child of a future generation? What right have I to borrow money which a future generation must pay back with interest, in order that I may now live?
I do not know how the home owner can continue to own his home. I do not know how the young man can buy a home, if the burden of taxation, which is greater than old Sinbad the Sailor ever carried on his shoulders, is permitted to continue. I should like to place on Hansard a submission made to the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations by the Canadian Chambers of Commerce on May 30, 1938.
71492-Hi
Real estate taxes.
At the time of confederation, wealth was represented mainly by land, and consequently the chief source of taxation was real estate. Times have changed, however, and wealth has come to exist in many forms. In more recent years, also, municipalities have had to bear a new financial responsibility in respect of social and welfare services which was not contemplated when their taxing powers were granted. The burden of these new services has fallen upon real estate to such an extent that the result has seriously affected the tendency of Canadians to own their own homes, retarded the construction industry, and undermined the value of investment in real property.
Last March, speaking about the federal responsibility for direct relief, I said:
I desire now to say just a word or two about the ability of the property owner in Hamilton to pay his taxes. In 1930 arrears of taxes in our city amounted to $1,107,710 against an assessment of $165,440,160. Seven years later what do we find? We have tax arrears to the amount of $2,488,555 on substantially the same assessment, or a trifle less, namely, $164,127,200.
I had the figures for 1938, but I appear to have mislaid them. They show a picture worse than that for 1937.
From the evening paper of to-day I read where the mayors' association has met in Toronto. Our Ontario mayors are trying to do a good job of setting their house in order, and to do so they need help from the federal government. I shall not read the whole of their resolution, but shall be content to record the two following paragraphs:
That the municipalities of Ontario, in the preparing of their 1939 budgets, absolutely refuse to budget for or pay in excess of thirty per cent of their actual expenditures for relief.
That in case the two governments contribute less than seventy per cent toward relief costs, the municipalities will cut relief to conform to the amount paid by them plus the thirty per cent contribution by the municipality.
We should pay attention to this mayors' association. They are setting their house in order, and they are trying to do a job that requires the cooperation of this government.
We must face up to another problem, and this is one for this and the next government. Surely there is room in the various phases of the administration of this government for the curtailment of expenses. Where shall we find it? Perhaps the railway problem furnishes food for thought. I shall not discuss it in detail, but let me say that thirty years ago the ordinary section gang was composed of six or seven men. Their job was to take care of five miles of track and roadbed. To-day three men constitute a section gang. We have not been practising economy from the top down. Four men in each gang have been put out of work, but I submit to the Minister
The Address-Mr. Marsh

of Transport (Mr. Howe) that he should focus his attention upon private cars, luxurious hotels and the general supervision of the railroad, instead of cutting down the section gangs. More money will be saved and more men will be given work on the tracks and in the roundhouses.
I should like to say a word or two about royal commissions, though previous speakers have already mentioned this matter. The government does not seem to have shown a flair for economy in the numerous royal commissions that have been appointed. This afternoon I was very much taken with the address of the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Fleming). While he was speaking I wanted to say, "Hurrah! for Ireland." He said that too many royal commissions had been appointed, and he advanced the argument that perhaps these commissions should be made up from members of this house. Certainly a commission should not be doing work that we as members of parliament are paid to come down here to do.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I said also that the members of the senate might be able to do it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I agree thoroughly with my hon. friend, and I should like to place on Hansard a short newspaper article about commission government. It says:
Actually, a royal commission represents the confession of a government that it doesn't know what to do about some given thing; or-what is just as bad-the confession of a government that it doesn't propose to do anything about a given thing. A. P. Herbert of Punch-
I may say that Mr. Herbert is a member of parliament as well as a humorist-
-hit the thing off perfectly in his famous poem:
I am the royal commission on Kissing,
Appointed by Gladstone in '74;
The rest of my colleagues are buried or missing;
Our minutes were lost in the last Great War.
But still I'm a Royal Commission,
My task I intend to see through,
Though I know, as an old politician,
Not much will be done if I do.
There is another problem which we have to face, which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) pointed out. This is a matter that concerns governments, present and future. Since 1930 Canada has spent $900,000,000 on relief. More and more it is being impressed upon the members of the House of Commons and upon thinking men throughout the country that relief without work is an unsound policy which results among other things, in a decadent manhood and womanhood, meanwhile placing a heavy burden upon the shoulders of the thrifty.
HVIr. Mavsh.J
I should like to say a word or two about the problem of youth. Last night when I should have been preparing this speech I went down to the railway committee room to attend the meeting in connection with the dominion-provincial youth program. We saw an interesting film entitled "Miners in the Making." I wish to compliment the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) upon the start he has made, but I suggest that this problem is so serious, so far-reaching and so affects the very fundamentals of Canadian life that we should not be simply puddling around in the shallows, we should be getting right down to the depths of this problem. I learned that 22,421 of both sexes had been trained, or rather had been enrolled, but that only 2,319 had been placed in industry. When you break up the total of 22,421, you find that 15,796 received physical training, which is quite worthy, but only 2,319 young men and women had been trained and placed in industry or other gainful employment.
I submit that the greatest investment in Canada is not our forests of white pine, yellow pine and pulpwood; it is not our mines of nickel, gold and radium; it is our Canadian youth. May I give some conservative figures concerning our youth problem, and I will underestimate rather than overestimate. I have it on good authority that 280,000 young men and women between the ages of sixteen and twenty-six are unemployed, and that of that number 72,000 have never had a job. Last year we voted $2,000,000 for the reestablishment of youth. Mr. Speaker, if an international crisis should arise and it should be necessary to defend our country, we would take that army of youth, put rifles on their shoulders and equip them for war. We would find $100,000,000, if necessary, to do it. Cannot we find $10,000,000 or $25,000,000 to equip this army for peace? If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) were in his seat, he would probably criticize me and say that I am inconsistent, in that, in one and the same breath I am suggesting a curtailment of expenditure and an additional expenditure.
My thought is this: We can take the young men of Canada and put them in employment camps. We can further, on a large scale, the work that has been started in afforestation and reforestation, in mining, in the building of roads up into the north country and on flood control projects; we can put them to work in the husbanding and re-creation of the resources of our country.
Now, if we solve our youth problem, if we solve our unemployment problem, we shall solve fascism, communism, nazism, and many

The Address-Mr. Marsh
other secondary problems that beset this dominion. If we do not solve these problems, then we cannot complain if a nation with iron in its blood comes in and possesses the land that we regard as rightfully ours.
The speech from the throne places a necessary emphasis on the question of national defence. When $33,000,000 was voted in 1937 for national defence, I think most of us thought that vote was wise. When $31,000,000 was voted in 1938, we thought it was wise. The government now announces that $60.000,000 will be spent on national defence. I think we should be proud of that vote. If the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) has not already done so, I should like him to take into consideration the recruiting of the material resources of the nation for national defence. It is just possible that our national defence is based on the standards of twenty or thirty years ago. I hope that when his estimates are brought down they will contain a vote for the establishment of a staff school in order that toolmakers, expert mechanics, captains of industry and others in the mechanical world may learn something about the making of 1939 ordnance. I hope it will never be necessary to fight a war in Canada or to defend our country, but the fact remains that the incidents of the last few months have been sobering.
I also hope that it will be made as easy as possible for military units throughout the country to attract the right kind of young men into the national service. I remember well bringing to the attention of the Minister of National Defence in the house last year the fact that staff officers in the various militia units had sometimes to bring in military accessories required by the unit from another country, because they could not be purchased in Canada, and I asked him if something might not be done to relieve them of the cost of paying sales tax and duty on these items. I pointed out then that we should not as a government try to make money out of a man's patriotism. The minister's answer was that the matter did not lie within his department but within the Department of National Revenue. I hope that in the meantime he and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Usley) have gone into a huddle in order to see that our good officers who are trying to build up their units do not have to pay money to the government for the privilege of being patriotic citizens.
Not long ago I went down to the armoury in Hamilton and I saw young lads wearing low oxfords, and they had stretched their
puttees down to try to cover them. The militia endeavours to build up their units by appealing to a man's pride in his personal appearance; yet one sees seven or eight different shades of khaki, ranging from a dirty yellow to a dark brown, and old boots that are worn out at the soles. I am not a military man, but I have heard it said that to have a good soldier you must keep him well shod and fill his stomach. Well, Mr. Speaker, some of those boys have not yet been able to find a job. They have not even a decent pair of boots in which to turn out on parade.
The motive force behind our militia units to-day is the veterans who served in the last war, and they deserve our best cooperation.
Just another word about equipment. How much of the equipment that you find in our armouries to-day is up to date? In Hamilton to-day in the armoury we have guns twenty-five years old. We have modernized them to the extent of putting pneumatic rubber tires on them, but they are still the same old guns. Concluding my remarks upon national defence may I say that the most valuable class of man power in Canada to-day, and I am sad to say it, is the returned veterans. They are better equipped to go to war because they know something about it, and it is too bad that our young men should not have been trained in national defence.
Just a word about the newly signed trade agreement. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) is reported in the Ottawa Journal of November 19 last as saying:
Employment would increase for two reasons: first, through greater activity stimulated in the primary industries:	second, through an
improved domestic market for Canadian manufactures, arising from the greater spending power of primary producers.
The minister knows as well as I do that the primary industries in this country employ only 100,000 people, while the secondary industries employ 900.000 people, or almost one million. It is the secondary industries that are going to suffer from this trade agreement. Take iron and steel, for instance. The national employment commission reported that manufacturers of iron and steel products, who should normally employ 100,000 people, had dropped 35,000 from their payrolls since 1929.	The trade agreement hits at the
secondary iron and steel industries. The imports in this- group from the United States amounted in 1937 to $22,000,000, subject to the old rate of duty which was thirty per cent. The new rate is the lowest ever. Take, for example, the basket tariff item for iron and steel products, 446A; the imports were $4,000,000 in 1933, and under the trade agreement of 1936 they rose to $10,000,000. With
The Address-Mr. Marsh

the lower duties in effect in the new agreement, where will the Canadian manufacturer of iron and steel fabricated products be? Our imports will double or treble under the new lower duties. The same applies to brass and copper products, imports of which jumped from $2,000,000 in 1935 to $3,000,000 in 1937; and to aluminum, imports of which jumped from $721,000 in 1935 to $1,727,000 in 1937. Again, machinery, exclusive of electrical apparatus and motor cars, was imported to the extent of $50,000,000 in 1937. This item represents the maximum of labour content, and yet the imports in many lines will double if parliament passes this trade agreement, So I say to the Minister of Labour that for every one extra employee engaged in primary industry

I am talking about the hewer of wood and the drawer of water-five artisans now engaged in the secondary industries will lose their jobs.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would point out that in the United States, and in Great Britain, before these trade agreements were signed, the authorities called into conference manufacturers and business men. They are the men who know what the effects of the agreements are likely to be on trade and industry. In Great Britain for example, there were called into consultation; Lord May, chairman of the import duties advisory committee; Sir Sydney Chapman and Sir Allan Powell, members of that same committee; also Sir Percy Ashley, the secretary. The federation of British industries was represented at the conference in Great Britain, and the Hon. Oliver Stanley, president of the British board of trade, was also called into consultation.
Finally. Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada are looking forward with unparalleled interest to the approaching visit of Their Majesties the King and Queen. May we see to it, above all else, that the boys and girls of this country see their king and queen? What do we matter? It is upon the shoulders of the younger generation that a greater and a better Canada is going to rest.
In the meantime may I beseech this government to shed its Rip Van Winkle mantle, arise from its long sleep, and bring down legislation early, so that when the king and queen come here in the month of May we shall have a better Canada to show them. Goodness knows, Canada needs a government.
On my way up to the chamber to-night I passed the parapet on which the snow had newly fallen, and two boys, seizing their opportunity, had written their names in the snow. They had seen their opportunity and had seized it. Never in the history of Canada, Mr. Speaker, has the extremity been so great, and never the

opportunity so present for writing bold and courageous laws for a new Canada. I say to the government: You have failed. You have come to the last page of the book, and the book is now about to be closed, with little having been done to better conditions in this country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I do not want to trespass on the valuable time of the house, I will be as brief as possible. First of all I should like warmly to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne on the excellent way in which they have performed their delicate task. May I also offer my most sincere congratulations to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for the splendid address he delivered the other night. Such a speech not only raised him still more in the esteem of his own followers, but, I am sure, made a profound impression on all hon. members. On the other hand, the speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) has been rather disappointing. I recognize that his duty is to criticize the actions of the government, but it would have been more in keeping with his position as party leader had he formulated constructive ideas instead of dwelling on the same old stories and launching mean attacks against the Prime Minister who will go down in history as one of Canada's greatest statesmen.
I listened with pleasure to the congratulations offered by the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier) to the prime minister of Great Britain for his action in the tragic days of the latter part of September. By these actions, Mr. Neville Chamberlain saved the world from the most appalling disaster. During those grim days, when the peace of the world hung by a thread, Great Britain, through her prime minister, made wonderful history.
Now, sir, I want to thank the government, on behalf of the victims of the terrible fire that destroyed the village of St. Luc de Matane, for the aid given them on that occasion. Those unfortunate people lost, in the course of a few hours, the result of several years of toil, labour and sacrifice. Thanks to the aid received from the provincial and federal governments, they once again feel confident and they will always keep the memory of the generous deed performed in order to help their village to rise from its ruins.
There is a question of great interest at the present moment on which I do not wish to dwell to-night, and that is the proposed admission in Canada of European refugees. However, I should like to avail myself of this

The Address-Mr. Lapointe (Matapedia)
opportunity clearly to define my attitude on that matter. For my part, I am unequivocally *opposed to the project. It is difficult enough, at present, to find work for our own unemployed without assuming new responsibilities.
I would fail in my duty as representative of the electoral district of Matapedia-Matane, were I to miss this opportunity of calling the attention of the government on the precarious situation in which our workmen find themselves during this winter. Owing to special circumstances, lumbering operations have been greatly reduced and accordingly a great number of workmen lost their livelihood. They are courageous men and what they are asking for is work. The government should start public works, without delay, especially in the industrial centres which suffer particular hardships.
The speech from the throne states the government's intention to expand its long range program of public undertakings as a means of relieving unemployment. I have already suggested to the government ways of ending this calamity in my section of the country.
My district offers great possibilities of development. Thousands of unemployed could be permanently established therein, but on condition that means of communication be provided, giving access to the interior of Matane county, which penetrates triangularly to the heart of Gaspe peninsula.
During the budget debate of the session of 1937 I had the honour of proposing to the government a five-year plan providing for means of communication giving access to immense forests which are going to ruin because of the ravages of the saw-fly and also because they have passed the age of maturity. Such a plan would also bring about the opening of a new territory eminently suited to colonization. During that debate I spoke as follows, on March 4, 1937, as recorded on Hansard:
Since we still have acute unemployment, since all the remedies which have been used so far have proved to be mere palliatives and have not given the expected results, since the calamity of unemployment threatens more and more to disorganize our economic system, why not consider a scheme for the development of our resources on a large scale? How many countries are there which would not like to own the wonderful heritage with which Providence has blessed us, in order to make it productive ?
Industry will never be able to absorb all our working men. Yet, it is imperative that we should give up the baneful policy of relief initiated by the former government, which has spoiled our people in teaching them to rely upon the nation for their upkeep.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, work is what is needed. Work for our honest unemployed who are courageous and find it humiliating to be
always appealing for help. Work for our young people who are losing their spirit through idleness.
Later, that is last year, when speaking, as I am now, on the address in reply to the speech from the throne and pleading before this house the case of our rural young people, I spoke the following words which are to be found in Hansard of February 1st, 1938:
When, looking at the map of my constituency,
I notice a vast district, comprising the townships of Laverendrye, Catalogne, Gravier, Clark, Casault, Lagrange, Bontet, Duniere, Richard, Cuocq, Leclere, Joffre and Baribault, which have never been opened to setlement,
I cannot but think that all the unemployed of my constituency could find work there. I reflect that there would be good prospects for all courageous and proud young men who are not afraid to face those hardships and sacrifices which, sooner or later, must be the lot of those who wish to succeed in life. I reflect that there would be good prospects for all our spirited young men in whose veins still flows the blood of the early settlers who opened to civilization the shores of the St. Lawrence. And I know, Mr. Speaker, that these young men are still numerous in my constituency, but they are awaiting the time when the government will open for them the way to those areas and help them to make a start.
Another essential undertaking closely connected with the development of my constituency is the improvement of Matane harbour, in order to make it as soon as possible a deep-water harbour. By its geographical situation Matane is destined to become a very important seaport. It is the natural outlet for the entire western section of Gaspe peninsula, including the interior.
Mr. Speaker, I know the people of my county. They are courageous and proud. They do not want charity; they want work. The government will, by granting my requests, contribute in a very large measure to the development of my district, while providing a large number of men now unemployed and penniless with the means of earning an honourable living.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, reference has been made by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Woodsworth), to the formalities at the opening but when the blowing of trumpets and the tumult and the shouting of the opening of parliament die, what will the harvest be for the working people of this country? It is not so much what the speech from the throne contains as what is left out. So far as any good to solve the economic problems of this country is concerned, it puts me in mind of old Mother Hubbard's cupboard. The government of the day have no constructive suggestions to give to the country how to solve the economic problems we have,
The Address-Mr. Church

and the duty is on the government of the day as long as they are the government to solve these problems. In a rich country like Canada, which has long been coveted by the dictators, with its magnificent natural resources, there should be nobody out of work. On the billboards during the last general election the government party made this reference to unemployment. "Vote Liberal and end unemployment." Well, all I know that they have ever done for unemployment is to find employment for a lot of useless commissions with their secretaries and lawyers and all that kind of thing. Right here in Ottawa they have established a great basic industry to solve the unemployment problem. It is known as the ambassadors' cure for unemployment, and ambassadors with three-cornered cocked hats, swords, epaulettes, spurs and all the rest of it are going to go to all the capitals on the seven seas to represent Canada. With its separatist policy, which this government is now pursuing, the appointment of all these ambassadors simply tends to separatist policies so fatal in war and destructive in peace. Reference has been made to the visit of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to Hitler in Berlin. The right hon. gentleman wanted to get Hitler's point of view, and he did; and Hitler certainly got the Prime Minister's point of view. Hitler knew how to shape his course when he discovered the separatist tendencies of the dominions. In the same way Emperor William in 1914, when he found a want of unity in the empire, after getting separatist views of South Africa and other dominions, decided to cross the Rhine, allowing treaties to become mere scraps of paper. And now Hitler is on the march. He has added Austria to Germany and is now going on to the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. Canada imposed sanctions against Italy and then repealed them, and after Ethiopia had been conquered, this foolish sanction policy drove Italy into the German orbit.
I find so many evasions and so many platitudes in the speech from the throne that I see no hope of the government's policy solving any of the economic, problems of the country. Reference is made in the speech to the coming of the king and queen. It is not the first time that the present king will have been in Canada. I saw him at the Falls before the war, when he was a midshipman, and at that time he showed a keen interest in the industrial progress of Canada and its people. On this occasion he will receive a hearty welcome from the Canadian people, not because there has been any change in his title. He is now being described by the high-
sounding title of King of Canada, but he has always been King of Canada. The British sovereign has been King of Canada ever since the treaty of 1763, so that high-sounding titles and coronations in India, Australia and elsewhere, which might satisfy the vanity of a few people who believe in the policy of separatism, are not at all necessary either by law, statute, usage or custom to make his majesty King of Canada. It seems to me that we are becoming more American than the Americans, and the capital of Canada is coming to be known as the Washington of the north, and Washington the Ottawa of the south. I doubt whether we have not been driven into the American orbit for keeps.
When the king does come to Canada I hope it will be recognized that the union jack is the only Canadian flag. It has been hauled down in South Africa and southern Ireland, but it has always been the flag of this country and I hope it will continue to be. Similarly, God Save the King is the only national anthem in Canada. It is both a hymn and a prayer, a prayer to the Almighty for the preservation of the king, the throne and the safety of his majesty's person and subjects. There has been no other national anthem in Canada since we have been a country. I was at a patriotic dinner function the other night, and at the conclusion the audience stood at attention and sang another anthem, O Canada, but that is not and was not the national anthem of Canada or our empire. I remember on one occasion when I was mayor of Toronto, some of those who attended a similar function in Massey hall, myself among them, declined to stand up when some other anthem was sung. As I say, there is only one national anthem for this country, and that is God Save the King.
We have lost one of the most brilliant men in the public life of Canada in the retirement of the former leader of this party (Mr. Bennett). He will sail at the end of this month for the old country, and I predict for him there, in the heart of the empire, as great a future as he has had a past in Canada. He is a marvellous man, a statesman and a patriot. He has been succeeded by our new leader (Mr. Manion), whom I have known since he was a medical student, who is very well liked, a man of good ability, a splendid type of Canadian, and in addition to that, one who is a returned soldier. I believe our new leader will give a great account of himself, as he has done already.
I should like to have seen in the speech from the throne a declaration in favour of the Christian religion in Canada. The Christian religion to-day, it seems, is being driven

The Address-Mr. Church
from pillar to post. Christianity is a part of the law of England, and by the constitutional act of 1791 it automatically became a part of the law of Canada. The National Conservative party of Mr. Chamberlain have made it a plank in their platform in England.
May I now say a few words with regard to the domestic policy of this government. After all, there is too much time and attention given to foreign affairs, since we are, as in 1812. for defence completely dependent on Great Britain. While foreign affairs are important, it must be remembered that we have to look after eleven million people in our own country, and I am surprised that in the speech from the throne there is not a single, definite, concrete proposal that promises any relief to the masses of the Canadian people, those whom Disraeli called the suffering millions. Canada has no policy but drift in matters of trade, defence and migration. In the speech from the throne there is no reference to these topics, nothing at any rate of a really concrete nature, though there are a lot of platitudes. One of the problems which this government has done nothing to solve is the problem of unemployment and distributism. What we should aim at is to restore Canada to the position she held under Macdonald, Laurier, Brown and Cartier. Canada was then a democratic country based and built upon the practical recognition of the principles of private property and freedom. But there is no freedom for the man who is at the mercy of arbitrary economic factors which are beyond his control.
One of the most important problems facing this country to-day was referred to in an address over the radio the other night, by the president of the Globe-Mail. Mr. McCullagh. namely the old way we have as a system of government. I believe this is the fourfold problem of constitutional, parliamentary, cabinet and law reform, and until these are satisfactorily dealt with we cannot have any economic reform. Let us take, first, constitutional reform. The constitution is three hundred years old. We have made no progress. As Mr. Grattan O'Leary said in a recent issue of Maclean's magazine, the executive have captured the government of Canada. It took over one hundred years of strife, turmoil and bloodshed for,the mother of parliaments to get control over the executive, but where is parliamentary control in Canada to-day so far as the expenditure of money is concerned? Nowhere. On February 17, 1937, I introduced a motion to provide that, instead of 245 members in this chamber holding a postmortem into the public accounts and estimates of the dominion, there should be estimate 71492-12
committees for the purpose. We should have the municipal system under which departmental heads could appear before an estimates committee and reductions made there. This,
I have no doubt, would result in a considerable saving to the people of Canada in the maintenance charges of the country. But the government will do nothing about it. The same apathy has marked their attitude to the questions of parliamentary, cabinet and law reform. We are behind the times so far as these important questions are concerned. Indeed, it seems to me our constitution is well on the way to be upside down at the present time. I should like to bring in a bill dealing with the question of referendums in Canada. Then the people would have some chance to rule. The referendum would be held on the same day as the general election, as in the case of the municipalities. In that way we might get some expression of opinion on two of the most important problems which this country is facing, over-government and over-taxation.
The municipalities had their revenues reduced in 1918 when the dominion government invaded the income tax field. In my opinion the federal power should assume the full cost of relief and should also give direct aid in connection with public health and hospital deficits. Canada spends about three and a half million dollars on the health of animals, but all it can spend on the health of humans is about S400,000. As I see it, the the first duty of a government is to look after the health, peace, welfare, comfort and prosperity of its people. The city of Toronto has spent $7,524,513 on relief, of which the city contributed over $2,700,000, the balance being divided between the federal and provincial governments. At a meeting of the Ontario mayors yesterday at Toronto it was stated that in future the municipalities might have to pay forty-five per cent of the cost of relief. If that should be so, the municipalities will face bankruptcy. In 1915, when I first became mayor of Toronto, seven and a half million dollars was all the money we had to spend in controllable expenditures. Real estate cannot stand any greater burden of taxation.
There is a bonus or subvention given to the city of Ottawa by this government in exchange for fire, police and water services. Every grant has a principle behind it, and in this case I believe the principle should be extended to the other large municipalities of Canada, all of which have federal public buildings within their boundaries, and give exactly the same kind of service.
Ontario has been most unfairly dealt with by this government. Under the Municipal

The Address-Mr. Church

Assistance Act, which was passed in the dying days of last session, provision was made whereby the municipalities could borrow money under certain conditions, if such loans were backed by the province. Owing to certain differences of opinion between the federal and provincial leaders of the Liberal party, how-iver, Ontario has been denied any relief in this direction, although Owen Sound wanted to build a city hall; Pelee township wanted to build a drainage system; Morrisburg wanted to build a school; London, a sewage system; Burlington, a water system; Kirkland Lake and Port Arthur, water and drainage systems, St. Thomas, a nurses' home; Gerald-ton, water and sewage systems; Hawkesbury, a school, hall and rink; Gravenhurst, a sewage system, and so on. These municipalities cannot qualify under that act because of the difficulty between the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Premier of Ontario. That is too bad, because I look upon the principle of confederation as being similar to that old Cornish battle-cry, "Each for all and all for each," and there should be equality of treatment as between the federal government and all the provinces on these relief measures.
A moment ago I was referring to the amount spent on the health of humans. Today, right down in ward 2, which the Prime Minister's grandfather once represented as mayor, there are many people who are in rags, starving, and living under terrible conditions. Reverend Mr. Wilson, pastor of King Street United Church, a very prominent man in Toronto, speaking at a luncheon recently said:
"We are striving to give the less fortunate boys and girls of the district a chance to gain a measure of success in life," declared Mr. Wilson. . . . "I have visited homes in this district where babies were born without even a towel to wrap around them," he told his listeners.
In my opinion the time has come for the dominion to increase its grants for public health, hospitalization, control of cancer, .and so on. How can the government look after the health and welfare of eleven million people if they spend only $400,000 a year on it?
I think it is time for a change, and I for one am sick of coming here and seeing such a bill of fare as is proposed in the speech from the throne, and all the hopelessness, inefficiency and do nothing policy in it.
I should like to offer one or two constructive suggestions to the government. I believe this country is afflicted with anglophobia on the radio, in the press and elsewhere. They have these debates over the radio, in the newspapers and elsewhere, by means of which (Mr. Church.]
people who do not even belong in this country can put before the people what they have to say in regard to foreign affairs. Such statements are full of half-truths, and they are believed by many who hear them. Our gaols are full of youths whose only fault is that they cannot find a job. There are forty-eight of these institutions in Ontario, and most of them have been condemned by a royal commission as unfit for human habitation. Last week I referred to a case in Timmins, where the magistrate sent seven high school boys to gaol for thirty days because they had no place to go, while he criticized the parliament of Canada in no uncertain terms for what it failed to do in not trying to solve the youth problem. Yesterday the youth council met in Ottawa. Some measure of relief for the youth of our country was adopted by this government after it had been suggested from this side of the house in 1936, 1937 and 1938. Many of us felt that the government in some way should utilize the services of the two hundred thousand youths who leave school every year, and that students in the universities and high schools might work in the summer in the development of our natural resources. That would be very much better than the export of brains from this country that has gone on in the past.
Even our history books are found wanting, in my opinion. Green, the great historian, whose History of England was Woodrow Wilson's favourite history, has been taken out of the high schools and other books substituted. I also believe greater care should be observed in the appointment of judges and magistrates, and that the bars should be consulted in regard to them. It is my belief the Magna Charta is becoming a dead letter in this country. People are sent to gaol for vagrancy, when they cannot get work, and there are fifty thousand youths roaming the country, riding the rods, looking for jobs. We have imprisonment for debt. Two years ago I introduced a bill asking that the law of England should be adopted here.
I believe that instead of abolishing appeals to the privy council, we should have some definite measure of law reform which would help the working people of this country, and lead to people not being sent to gaol for debt or imprisonment without bail, in most instances.
Recently the Toronto Globe referred to bylaws which are passed by federal commissions. This parliament confers on commissions and officials of the government the power to make rules and regulations, which even this parliament has not power to enact, and which are thus given the force of statute. In my

The Address-Mr. Church
opinion, these by-laws and regulations should not be passed until they have been approved as being intra vires by the Department of Justice, which gives legal advice to the government and the various commissions which it creates.
I notice that there has been some talk in the Ottawa newspapers to the effect that the east and west blocks, those historic relics of confederation, which have housed the brains of our country and where the privy council has met since we have been a country, should be torn down. To some people the past seems nothing but error, but I look upon it as modern desecration to see such buildings and memorials torn down and replaced by others, when at one time they housed the best brains of Canada and great men like Macdonald, Laurier, Tupper, Borden, Bennett, King and Meighen.
I might say something about the high cost of living. As a matter of fact I should have expected something about the high cost of living in the speech from the throne. Three years ago there were some references sent to the tariff board for an inquiry having to do with motor cars, motor trucks, radios and other articles. What has happened to those references?
