When will parliament see the reports? I have received letters from my constituents, but I have seen no results of the efforts of the board. These letters complain that radios, motor cars, motor trucks and refrigerators cost thirty-five per cent less in the city of Detroit than they do in Windsor. I believe in adequate protection; I am strong for it; but I also believe that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) should place in the tariff schedules regulations whereby the manufacturer would get a fair profit on his capital, leaving some protection for the consumer and labour.
After all is said and done, where is the enemy of protection? The enemy lies in about five per cent of the manufacturers who want to grab all the benefits for themselves, and leave nothing for labour or the consumer. I believe some returns have been made in the interim by the tariff board to the minister, and something should be done along this line.
I have read where the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has made some observations. May I add in passing that we were pleased to see him at the winter fair. In his speech in Montreal he made some observations about unemployment. If he had studied the Couzens report made to the United States senate and Mr. Purvis' report made to parliament a year ago, he would have found that unemployment in many forms will always be with us. There will 71492-12j
always be large numbers who will not find work. I suggest the minister would be far better employed if he urged the government to give us some relief in connection with the intolerable conditions which now exist.
In the time left at my disposal I should like to refer to foreign affairs, to the Chamberlain policy, to the experience which has been gained through history, to pacifism and to education as they relate to these problems. I do not agree with the policy of silence in Canada about foreign affairs and about Canada's defence policy as set out in the speech from the throne. " Trust the people " should be the policy. The policy of silence has been condemned in England and the world over. If Britain fails, the whole world will go with it into outer darkness. The peoples of the empire and of the world will lose civilization, freedom, peace and the freedom of religion we enjoy. I am opposed to a policy of spineless pacifism and to the continuous making of pacifist speeches. I am opposed to a policy of letting the old country go it alone and bear the whole burden of the costs.
Let us not forget the lessons of history in connection with these matters. It was the armed strength of the barons and the suppression of tyranny in the days of King Johr which made Magna Charta possible. The disarmament of the free is the tyrant's chance now as it was in the days of King John. Guardians of freedom must always be on guard. So far as Canada is concerned, may I point out that an unarmed Britain simply invites invasion and insult and, in the end, extinction. Before God to-day Britain stands as the trustee for the peace of the world, but she cannot go it alone. Other states of Europe, the smaller states, look to England as if she were the policeman of the world. But she cannot do it alone, because these weaker and smaller states now follow Germany; they simply follow the leader or the crowd.
Great Britain seeks no conquest for herself, but wishes only to establish the Kingdom of God on earth and to bring about a greater freedom of religion and of civilization, a freedom of the press and of the pulpit, of the legislatures and of the universities.
If one were to accept the views of the Prime Minister and his officials in the Department of External Affairs, one might be led to the conclusion that they were conducting their own foreign policy, a policy of silence. That policy has been condemned in the British House of Commons. According to a report in the Times of March 18. 1938, Mr. Neville Chamberlain, Prime Minister of Great Britain, speaking before the parliamentary press gallery, said:
The Address-Mr. Church

If the people are not allowed to know the facts; if they are not allowed to know what their rulers choose them to know, then that people are in danger of being led to embark upon a course which may presently lead them into disaster.
Then, on March 24, the Prime Minister in the British House of Commons defined the commitments of Great Britain which might lead to armed intervention for purposes other than our own defence or the defence of possessions within the empire. In the course of his statement he said:
There remains another case in which we might have to use force, under the covenant of the League of Nations to bring help to a victim of aggression, even though there should be no direct obligation to take such action.
Since those words were spoken, many things, for the greater part disastrous for us, have happened. Many policies are dead. Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Daladier, when signing the Munich agreement, drove the last nails into the coffin of the League of Nations. It is time the Prime Minister of Canada permitted the people to know the facts of the situation:	A policy of silence is condemned
by the Minister of War in the British House of Commons, the Right Hon. Leslie Hore-Belisha; it is his view that it is better to be candid than to conceal the truth. He went so far as to tell the British House of Commons about the deficiency in the defence preparations in the city of London. He said they were not prepared for a war, and that Great Britain would have to make greater sacrifices. Edmund Burke said that government is a practical thing and not an agency to please and aid the fancy problems of ordinary politicians.
Before the war of 1914 Lord Roberts asked for more defences. I can recall no more sad or tragic spectacle in the history of the British empire than Lord Roberts pleading for an armed Britain, and that something be done about armaments. But he was laughed at by leaders in the government. He died in the early days of the war, but lived long enough to see his prophecy fulfilled, and to hear the sound of the guns. It is admitted that if his advice had been taken and the facts known of war near at hand, England would have had 400,000 men ready when Germany engaged in the first battle of Ypres, with a further 120,000 reservists for each additional year, and the fortunes of war would have been different. But before the British forces were ready, the western front had frozen into the deadlock of trench warfare, which was to last for almost three more years.
If democracies are to be preserved, then all Canada must accept certain sacrifices. It is

worth while, when we realize the awful possibilities of last September. The people of Canada should know the facts. So far as Italy is concerned, sanctions were invoked, but were not enforced. I say that this government has adopted a policy of isolation.
Do we remember the isolationist and pacifist speeches made in the House of Commons in 1937 and 1938 by government members from the province of Quebec? Do those speeches now represent the policy of the government? Have they a different policy on foreign affairs and defence for each province in the dominion? I think the people in Canada are entitled to know what the policy may be before it is too late. It is all very well to depend upon the United States; we welcome them, but I am here to say that the Johnson act will prevent Hitler, France or Great Britain from floating loans in the event of war. On top of that there is a resolution about munitions. The policy of the United States government is well known. At the present time America speaks with two voices. One is the ambassadorial voice of the president and the other is the congressional voice of the senate and the house of representatives who have the say. I believe that Canada has been criminally negligent in defence matters. A national survey should be made of our man power, our industrial power, our food power and everything like that.
They are critical about Chamberlain at Munich, but he did all that could be done I know of no dominion more responsible for that policy of disarmament than Canada which urged it. They scrapped the finest ail force, the finest navy and the finest army the world had ever seen. That was MacDonald-ism. What was the result? You cannot build up a force like that in a day or a generation. The result was that Great Britain was found to be unarmed. Mr. Chamberlain saved civilization and the world at Munich. It may be only a postponement, but he did all that was possible until Britain is fully armed.
What are we doing about youth in this country? I gave the government a policy last year. The Hon. Ernest Brown, Minister of Labour in England, has been trying to get them to do something for youth over there. His policy is set out in a report which appeared in the Times of September 11. He made a tour of the unemployment centres. Speaking at a civic luncheon held in the town hall at Liverpool, he said:
Last month, between the ages of 18 and 24, there were 74,034 unemployed in Liverpool, Bootle, Birkenhead and Wallasey. Assuming that one-third of these young men, say 24,700 are physically fit to join the army-if one-third should not be fit, what a reflection on our public health and education authorities-*

The Address-Mr. Church
This is what he should have said to the young men, according to the National Review:
Look here, young fellows! Employment is vailing for you in the army. If you take it you will get food and clothing; free housing; pocket-money; instruction and physical education; you can learn a trade, if you have not already mastered one, at a vocation centre before your seven years' service are up; also, while serving, you will earn deferred pay. You can widen your outlook by going abroad, and you can qualify yourselves to enter Sandhurst and get commissions. You may have heard a prime minister emphasize the slogan "Safety first." Young men! it is safer to be in the army than to walk on a public road in England. We lay these conditions before you. Should you decide not to take advantage of them, you must get a living wage elsew-here; but do not expect your fellow men who are at work to contribute to your maintenance and idleness.
I do not propose this policy for Canada, far from it; but I do contend that this government, having spent $900,000,000 on unproductive relief, should consult industry and labour as to a policy, adapted to Canada's special circumstances for our youth now on the dole.
I am not suggesting anything compulsory; it should all be voluntary. We should have a suitable Canadian apprenticeship system like what they have in England. Our youth should be given an opportunity to learn a trade as well as obtaining other education; they should set part time employment and part-time education. They should be able to obtain at least a little pocket money, clothing, food, a home, deferred pay and security, instead of being forced to go round filling up the prisons of this country. A Presbyterian divine speak-_ug in Toronto yesterday said that unemployment is the main reason why so many of our vnufh find themselves in our gaols.
This government has negotiated a treaty with the United States but it is simply a political treaty. We have lost the British preference of six cents per bushel on wheat which we obtained after twenty-six years. This preference was granted to Canada, Australia and the other dominions, but it has been taken away. We have also lost the three per cent excise tax. That means a loss of $18,000,000. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) should be providing for that in his budget, and then the government should use this money to relieve real estate and the municipalities, and increase our social services, as I have suggested and as has been suggested also by the head of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Woodsworth). Something should be done along that line.
Something should be done for our youth. Some of the brightest minds in the country are to be found in our high schools; yet many of these youths are simply riding round the
country. They come from some of the finest homes in Canada, but quite often they find themselves in gaol simply because the only thing against them is that they cannot get a job. I think the time will come when it will be shown that this agreement with the United States is very bad for this country. We have given up our preference on wheat in the British market which may never be regained. Governor Landon and the republican party are pledged to the repeal of this treaty. What will be the result when that happens? We shall have lost our preference, and our steady market in Great Britain, our best customer. Canada and the other dominions will be driven into the Washington orbit, and I fear that *Washington will become the economic centre of the British Empire. The government has no policy along other lines. The policy of the government in reference to this treaty has been condemned by many capable authorities, and I shall probably have something to say again in connection with it.
I am sorry to see that politics and spending of money like water have again entered into the operation of the Canadian National Railways. The government has given its consent to the completion of the new terminal at Montreal at a cost of over twelve million dollars. I should like to read some questions that I now ask the government here in this debate:
X. Has the government given its consent to the proposed completion of the new Montreal terminal of the Canadian National Railway and at what cost and on whose recommendation was the work asked for started?
2.	Will any plan of the said work be tabled and the reports relating thereto?
3.	Was parliament asked to sanction said work and when?
4.	Is the work to aid relief and relieve unemployment?
5.	Did the government meet the corporation of the city of Montreal on the subject or others ?
6.	Does the province of Quebec contribute anything to the cost of the work or were they asked under relief and municipal assistance legislation to sanction or aid said work?
7.	What sums have already been spent on this work and by whose authority?
8.	Has the board of transport for Canada been asked to sanction such huge expenditures or report on them or their necessity as recommended by-
(a)	Drayton-Acworth report.
(b)	The Duff report on railways.
9. Will the cost of said work be raised by taxation from income or capital or will it be raised from income from sales or income tax or will part of it be raised for relief works by the government ?
10.	What efforts were made at coordination or to eliminate deficits before such work was started ?

The Address-Mr. Church
11.	Have any objections to such an uneconomic work been received and from whom?
12.	Will any reports on relief or the necessity of relief works of this kind be tabled and will other cities receive similar aid of unemployment relief works and be heard direct by the government instead of being directed to the provinces under the municipal assistance relief legislation?
13.	What reports are in existence as to the financial, economic and engineering features of the work ?
14.	Will preference be given to Canadian labour and Canadian industries in its construction ?
15.	What other purely municipal relief undertakings and works in Montreal have been undertaken by the government either above or in conjunction with the province for the last three years of record?
16.	Does the action taken or to be undertaken now supplement the provisions made by the Honourable the Ministers of Public Works and Secretary of State during the winter of 1938 in the by-elections for the House of Commons in the district of Montreal and reported fully by Canadian press at the time?
Again we are to have politics and inefficiency in the Canadian National Railways. There is very weak management in that road. With a deficit of $50,000,000, I am sure the people of this country will oppose this extravagance which is not necessary from an engineering or financial or railway standpoint, and we should have a joint committee of both houses of parliament to try to solve this railway problem. I made this suggestion last year, but the government rejected it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, practically four days have been taken up with this debate; the flow of oratory still continues and the end is not in sight. It becomes increasingly difficult for those of us who are on the back benches to contribute much in the way of constructive thought so late in a debate of this kind. The leaders of the two main political parties have gone over the issues so thoroughly and carefully and have taken up so much time in doing so that those of us who are compelled to follow them find it almost impossible to make the contribution we would like to make.
The mover (Mr. Matthews) and seconder (Mr. Chevrier) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne are to be congratulated upon the excellent manner in which they carried out their tasks. Their speeches show what can be accomplished by speakers when the range of subjects has not been curtailed in any way by those who have preceded them. I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) upon the speech he made on Tuesday. He always contributes something constructive to

every debate in which he takes part. I want to say the same to the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Fleming) who spoke this afternoon. I cannot agree entirely with all they said, but their remarks upon monetary reform were of special interest to me.
It is always a source of amusement to me,, when I hear the leader of the government or the leader of the opposition or a private member speak about the result of a by-election. It is always looked upon either as an endorsement or condemnation of the policies of the government. The mover of the address (Mr. Matthews) stated that the voters of Brandon had emphatically endorsed the platform of the Liberal party by returning a Liberal member. He said that his election was generally looked upon as an endorsement of Liberal policies by the people of western Canada. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) was quick to cite the by-election in Waterloo South as showing the attitude of the east. I well remember when the Edmonton East by-election was fought. Some cabinet ministers before the election result was announced were foolish .enough to state that the result would clearly indicate how the west felt about Liberal policies; but when the result was actually known, we heard nothing about the west or what it had to say about the party system in general, or about the Liberal party in particular. I think it would be just as well if we dropped this old line of talk because it has been worked so long and so often that people are getting tired of hearing it.
I was very much interested in the computation which was made by a member of the Conservative party of the length of the speech from the throne this session. He told us that he had compared this speech with other speeches on similar occasions and found that the speech this year was the longest for many years past. The leader of the opposition, as reported at page 22 of Hansard, said:
In spite of all the criticism that has been heaped upon these two parties, I believe that they have done fairly well in the government of Canada throughout these years.
An interesting computation which might be undertaken by the same Conservative member, or by a Liberal for that matter, would be to calculate what these two parties have contributed towards the debt of this country since 1870, during the last seventy years since confederation. It might also be of interest if the same gentleman would compute what Liberal and Conservative governments in the provinces have contributed by way of debt to the debt structure of the provinces. The total is astounding. On January 1, 1936, the

The Address-Mr. Marshall
total debt of municipalities, provinces, and the dominion stood at $6,950,000,000; in round figures; on January 1, 1937, it had amounted to S7,249,000.000; on January 1, 1938, it had reached a total of $7,267,000,000; on January 1, 1939, according to the information I have here it had risen to a grand total of $7,449,000.000. And now there stands on the order paper a resolution in the name of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) asking parliament to give him authority to borrow, by way of loan, the sum of $750,000,000.
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, from whom that money will be borrowed. We hear a great deal about the widows and orphans in this country. I wonder if they have anything to contribute towards this loan. In my humble judgment, they have already contributed all they had towards loans in the past. I do not think any private individual or any group of individuals has enough money to make up the amount of this loan. But I believe that it will be borrowed from the creators of money and credit, the biggest legal racketeering concerns in the country, the bankers and their allies and associates, the financial institutions. And finally, in due course, the people of Canada will be called upon to foot the bill by way of taxation; and the interest, which is not created at the time the principal is created, will have to be found as well. I think the day is not far distant when the people of this country will call for an accounting from these two old parties, and in due process of time I believe they will go out of existence just as the snow vanishes before the summer's sun.
I listened with careful attention to the leader of the opposition as he "cussed" and discussed the policies of the present government. Most of his criticisms were merited, but I should like to say to him in a kindly way that his speech was more destructive than constructive. It appeared to me that we were witnessing the same old drama that has been played so often during the last seventy years, of the pot calling the kettle black. That is exactly what it amounted to, and I can assure the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that their speeches deceived no one, particularly those of independent mind who do their own thinking. for their speeches were nothing but smoke screens.
I should like to make a few comments on one item which was discussed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Col dwell) and later referred to by the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman). It is true that the matter was touched upon this afternoon by a member of my own group, but I
offer no apology for reopening it. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar described very carefully and exhaustively the benefits which had accrued to the people of the Dominion of New Zealand through legislation which had been enacted by a labour government, a government which went into power in the year 1935 and was reelected in 1938. He stated further that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group of which he is a member was advocating the adoption of measures similar to those carried out in New Zealand. Let me assure him that this group of which I am a member are advocating similar measures, but with certain provisos. I assume that were the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation to take over the government of any province or even the government of Canada, they would follow along lines similar to those in our sister dominion. Let me hasten to assure the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation that in spite of the fact that Major Douglas, the father and founder of the social credit philosophy, visited New Zealand some years ago and conferred with leading men in that country, we as social crediters do not claim that this philosophy is being practised in New Zealand at the present time. The government of New Zealand has not yet-and I use the word " yet " advisedly-commenced to put any social credit principles into effect; so that we as a group will not quarrel with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar if he claims New Zealand for the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. However, I believe there are certain facts which he in particular and the country in general should know. It is a well known fact that the labour party was returned to power in 1935, and they obtained on that occasion fifty-three seats out of a possible eighty. How was that election won? That is the question. I propose to read a paragraph from an article which was published in the New English Weekly, London, England. The first paragraph reads:
A lifetime spent in New Zealand, including the first six months of the present labour government's regime, enables me to endorse the claim of the latter to be the first labour government in the British empire elected to power as well as to office.
Standing on the main plank cif monetary reform, this government rode to victory by an overwhelming majority in November, twelve months ago. That election was notable, for every daily paper of any consequence was actively engaged in opposition, and an unprecedented amount of money was poured out for propaganda of the most violent nature by the banks.
This is the part to which I wish to draw special attention:
Yet the counter-effect of two to four years' hard spade-work by over three hundred social
The Address-Mr. Marshall

credit groups throughout New Zealand was sufficient to immunize the electors when it came to the test.
I notice that when I mentioned the New English Weekly, some hon. members on the opposite side of the house seemed to think it quite a joke. Perhaps that is not a very responsible magazine from which to take an article, and perhaps one might question its authenticity; but I have before me the report of a speech which was made in the city of Edmonton, and the authenticity of which no hon. member, more particularly my hon. friends sitting to my right, can doubt. In the summer of 1938 a splendid young woman from Edmonton visited New Zealand. I do not know her particularly. I know of her; I know that she is a woman of culture and intelligence. She is a teacher in that city. She went to New Zealand and studied conditions there carefully. Her name is Miss Mary R. Crawford, and she is the treasurer of the Alberta Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. In her opening remarks she had this to say:
The people of New Zealand have the light of social justice shining out brightly upon them, and compared to them we are laggards. I think it is time we began to catch up.
Going on with her talk, she said;
Social credit has been a corridor through which thousands of New Zealanders had marched to an acceptance of labour principles.
But, she said, social credit had not elected a single candidate in the 1935 election. That is very true, because social credit did not put any candidates in the field in that election. Continuing, she said this:
People in New Zealand were vitally concerned with monetary problems, and social credit apostles had served to heighten this already acute interest by their crusade.
So I think that we as a group of social crediters should be given some credit for the victory of the labour party in the 1935 election. Some of the legislation which has been enacted by that government since they were elected in 1935 has been, to say the least of it, wonderful. These are some of the things they have done:
A basic minimum weekly wage fixed by government decree of approximately twenty dollars, taking the pound's value as five dollars. In addition, an arbitration court must see that wages allow an adult male worker "to maintain a wife and three children in a fair and reasonable standard of comfort."
All citizens in New Zealand are entitled, as of right, to complete, universal, free medical and hospital care from general practitioners. This includes full maternity benefits, as well as special provisions for invalids of a minimum of five dollars per week for an adult incapacitated for work.

The forty-hour, five-day working week, without any loss of wages.
Old age pensions payable at the age of sixty instead of seventy as in Canada. The pension is more than 1J times as much as that here.
I should like to see, and every member of this group would like to see, this government bring in legislation to provide for old age pensions for people at the age of sixty, yes, and even lower than that.
A system of unemployment insurance already in force.
The government pays a guaranteed price to dairy farmers-back-bone of agriculture in New Zealand-and the price must remain stable the whole year. It also set up a primary products marketing department to handle the export and sale of dairy produce. The government owns all dairy produce intended for export and takes the loss, if any, itself. Profit goes to the farmer.
Farm hands obtain a month's holiday with pay each year.
These are some of the amenities of life which have been brought to the people of New Zealand by the labour government, and I, for one, heartily commend that government for what they have done. But I take exception to the manner in which these blessings have been brought about. Let me quote again from Miss Crawford's speech-and in my opinion this lady is just as good an authority as can be found anywhere. This is what she says:
This elaborate social service program, Miss Crawford explained, is financed by a charge of one pound per person to register for these benefits, plus a further tax of one shilling in every pound upon all wages, salaries and income.
To my mind that is where the nigger is in the wood pile. These amenities have been brought to the people of New Zealand by means of an elaborate system of taxation. It takes $5 to register, five per cent, or one shilling in every pound, of wages, salaries and income. It is my firm belief that these blessings can be brought to the people of Canada, and they must be brought to the people of Canada, without an increase in taxation. I believe this can be done through the medium of controlling the currency and credit of the country and using that currency and credit in terms of the public need. They are not doing that in New Zealand at the present time, and that is the point. That is where we, as social crediters, do not agree with the prime minister of that dominion. The hon. member for Huron North said, in the course of his remarks:
... I suggest that hon. members keep these things in their memory-

The Address-Mr. Lalonde
Things which he had spoken of earlier in his speech.
-for a year or two and then pass judgment when the test of time has brought its result.
Well, he is not foolish enough to think that Premier Savage is going to remain idle, doing nothing within the next year or two. When Premier Savage spoke at Auckland before 8,000 people, he said:
. . . money must be provided for production, and money must be provided for consumption. Unless a country could buy what it produced, trade expansion was impossible.
. . . unless the government of a country controlled the credit of the country it could not control anything else.
It is therefore my humble but firm judgment that the battle which should have been commenced in 1935 by the Premier of New Zealand is just beginning now. He is just about to find the stillest opposition of his life when he comes to fight those who control the currency and credit of his country.
May I now for a moment speak to one who used to have a seat very close to these two reform parties. I realize that the matter is not covered by the speech from the throne; but if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will leave his Beauchesne's Par-liamentry Rules and Forms in his desk for a little while and forget about it, I shall take a few minutes to say what is on my mind.
I am sorry that the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) has moved over from these groups. I do not believe he will be happy with his former love unless his party makes far-reaching changes in their program. In the last session of this parliament, on March 31, 1938, he had the following to say. I quote from page 1911 of Hansard. Speaking of the price of cattle he said:
There is serious distress; in fact, the interjection of the minister tempts me to point out that the price of cattle to the farmers in Canada is not a fair price or one based upon the law of supply and demand at all. It is fixed in Toronto by the heads of the packing institutions, and that condition is unfair to the farmers. I am going to have more to say about that later on. I feel strongly on this question, because next to grain, if not indeed equally with grain, the marketing of live stock is one of the largest items in the production of newr wealth in this country. There is no question in my mind-and I have given the matter a great deal of study-that the farmers of Canada are to-day, and have been-I was going to use the word "defrauded"-deprived, and unjustly deprived, of millions of dollars annually that they should get. I am prepared to prove that, and I shall do so one of these days. I am almost tempted to proceed with an analysis of these conditions, but I did not rise for that purpose to-night. When it is suggested that these conditions apply to other commodities, that is true, but there is nothing in the whole realm of activity in Canada to-day
comparable with the unfairness in connection w'ith marketing live stock.
Then he was followed by the Minister of Agriculture who said:
With regard to the last few remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay East, while there may be a great deal of truth in the statement that we are not obtaining enough for our cattle. I think it is pretty well agreed, particularly by those of us who are raising cattle, that there is a feature of the present situation which should be mentioned u'hen we are discussing it from that point of view'.
May I say to the hon. member for Kootenay East that these w'ords of his are known to every farmer and every cattleman in Alberta. They were the subject of a long discussion on the floor of a convention held in the city of Calgary under the auspices of the rural municipal districts association, where a resolution was passed calling upon the government to take immediate action. I hope the hon. member will take the earliest opportunity- perhaps during this debate

to lay bare all the facts, as they are known to him. Should he succeed in getting action in remedying this abuse, I can assure him that he will win the gratitude certainly of all cattlemen living in Alberta and, I am sure, of all cattlemen in the west.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to repeat what the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) said in this house during the session of 1936:
Now may I say a w'ord by way of reminder, because I want to warn the government and the Liberal party to-day that if I am right in my conclusions as to the way in which the public has interpreted these promises that w'ere made as pledge before election, if they are not fulfilled then it may be that the Liberal party is placing its footsteps on that trail of broken promises which leads not only through the valley of humiliation but down deep into the abysmal depths of eternal oblivion.
I want to bring those w'ords back to the minds of hon. gentlemen sitting to your right, Mr. Speaker. I want to tell them that danger-signals are flying all over this country, and I hope the Liberal party will heed those signals before it is too late.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although by tradition the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne is an occasion for one side of the house to exalt the policies of the government and for the members of the opposition to decry them, the words of praise that I shall have for the government are in no way dictated by that custom, but by the government's record itself. In rising to speak on behalf of the county of Labelle I am performing a duty commanded by justice and equity.
The Address-Mr. Lalonde

I hold it as a principle that it is the duty of all Canadians to preach and practise Canadian policies. I submit that the policy enunciated in the speech from the throne and which has been preached and practised for the past three years by the government of this country is essentially Canadian and that therefore it is the duty of every patriot to give it his loyal and sincere support. It is unnecessary, Mr. Speaker, to dwell on the first -of these statements. According as our young country, in the course of time, acquires the characteristics and forms of an independent state; according as through the slow but natural evolution of its national life, it obtains its majority rights and takes at the concert of nations the place of honour to which it is entitled; according as on its territory there develops a population deeply rooted in traditions of order and of peace; according as Canada, through her immense natural resources and the work of her children, increases her influence among the nations of the world, every Canadian worthy of the name owes it to his country and his race to promulgate and put into practice just and reasonable laws and a truly Canadian policy.
I say that the policies of the present government, taking into account what economists call intangible factors and what I would call unforeseeable factors, are truly Canadian.
There is only one policy worthy of that name, and that is liberalism as we, federal Liberals, understand it. Far be it from my mind to advocate that partly political and partly religious liberalism, or, if you wish, that partly economic and partly religious liberalism which our opponents, especially in the province of Quebec, are prone to connect with the liberalism of Laurier. By Canadian liberalism, I mean the political doctrine which glorifies individual freedom as far as it can promote individual and social welfare. Set against excessive nationalism of which it is the absolute antithesis, such a doctrine curbs the arbitrary demands of the powerful and the pundits by promoting free and legitimate competition. Canadian political liberalism owes its existence and its principles to French liberalism which, at the outset, was opposed to the absolute power of monarchy. Under the Restoration, it was the policy of those who fought the government of Louis XVIII and Charles X and sought the return of the conditions prevailing after 1789. Victorious in 1830, liberalism became conservative in 1848, as it was then opposed to socialism. Since then, liberalism has been the name assumed by parties advocating civil and political liberty and fighting extreme theories, whether of the right, the center or the left. To-day it is

particularly the policy of those who fight state socialism, antireligious sectarianism and all attempts at dictatorship springing either from the right, the center or the left. It is, in a word, sir, the antithesis of toryism whose sole ideal has always been, particularly in this country, the protection of the privileged classes at the expense of the masses.
The foregoing statements lead us to the conclusion that liberalism as practised in Canada provides the ground for the full flowering of practical and theoretical freedom in the economic field. In conclusion, it can be safely stated that, in safeguarding the liberty of man and his most cherished aspirations which include his complete freedom of thought and speech, our political liberalism stands as the irreducible opponent of autocracy, of monopoly and of dictatorship.
Set against the dictatorial nationalism and excessive racism condemned by the Pope himself, our political liberalism has been able to accomplish great things for our beloved country. It has created and built up the code of a truly Canadian policy, as we shall see.
It is under a liberal government that our country conquered its sovereignty, later consecrated by the Statute of Westminster in 1931. It was by affirming the doctrine of reciprocity in 1911 that Laurier, with a display of self-abnegation which will go down in history as one of the most moving of all political sacrifices, became an exponent of the purest liberalism. Then in 1935 his successor, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), continuing the tradition, negotiated the first treaty of reciprocity with the United States, thus destroying the remaining vestiges of absolute protectionism so dear to the heart of our Tory opponents. Finally, on November 17, 1938, the prime minister signed in Washington a second treaty of reciprocity which will stand as the climax of the sovereignly human accomplishments due to the political liberalism of the present government of Canada.
I could praise this treaty by pointing to its beneficial results for the farmers and lumbermen of my constituency, as it will open a great market for our agricultural products and will tend, by a freer export of forest products, to reduce the latent unemployment existing in that part of the province as a result of a considerable reduction in lumbering operations. But the treaty will do more than that. In addition to its practical effects and its important pecuniary advantages, it will become one of the effective means of strengthening national unity in our country.
It is no secret that this unity is threatened. Underhand campaigns of chauvinism and separatism inspired by a presumptuous egoism

The Address-Mr. Lalonde
have shaken the structure of confederation. Inhabited by people of different races and religions. Canada has to fight to maintain its national life.
It is greatly to the credit of the Prime Minister and his government to have been able to accomplish the marvellous feat of maintaining in stable equilibrium these contrary forces and dissimilar interests and to make of all these heterogeneous parts a viable whole that is called Canada. Amendments and additions will soon have to be made, in order to adapt the terms of the federative agreement to the needs of-the various groups. Without destroying anything, we should seek to build a finer and larger structure. I am confident that the present government of this country will safeguard the rights of the Catholic and French minorities and guarantee them the full exercise of their privileges. Our national unity which was threatened by the world crisis is stronger and livelier than ever, following the setbacks of nationalism and the victories of the present government's political liberalism. This treaty, affecting the most cherished interests of all the classes constituting the great Canadian nation, will re-establish this spirit of solidarity and unity on more solid bases.
In the international field, the policy of the present Liberal government has been Canadian.
There may be some who prefer to the thoughtful and prudent statesman some buffoon of present-day politics. I prefer the wisdom of the present Prime Minister to the saucy verbosity of some of his opponents.
When the European dictators, driven by the imperious necessity of a display of strength essential to the maintenance of their prestige, and swollen by a pagan racism, had Europe within an ace of war; when in a moment of folly they demanded, gun in hand, further ransoms and further conquests, the entire Canadian people stood in those tragic hours behind the traditional serenity of their Prime Minister who had promised that parliament alone would decide the question of Canada's participation in foreign wars. This statement, Mr. Speaker, is the consecration of the Liberalism of Laurier such as we practise it.
A certain Montreal daily newspaper sought in its edition of January 18th, 1939, to spread about the government and its leader a falsehood that common sense itself will refute. Because the Prime Minister of Canada read passages of a book which quoted a statement of Sir Wilfrid Laurier who had said in 1910 that when England is at war Canada is at war, this paper concluded that the leader of the government was ready to launch the country in an adventure of military conscription should England be drawn into a conflict. It took good care, though, not to quote in full Laurier's words, which were these: "When England is at war we are at war and exposed to attack." That is an altogether different matter and, besides, in 1910 the imperial tie was an all-powerful factor. Our colonial and dependent status implied certain obligations on our part, and bound us, as it were, to the mother country's destiny. But the wonderful emancipation brought about by the statute of Westminster freed us from that responsibility. Had the leader of this government issued such a fateful proclamation, our very independence would have been sufficient to ensure our right to declare our neutrality. But there is no need to give more publicity to that misleading announcement. Further on, the same newspaper admits that the policy of this government as regards participation in foreign ware is that parliament, only is supreme, not the government. I am not surprised that the semi-official organ of the nationalists in Quebec should have availed itself of this opportunity to do some hair-splitting in order to launch an anti-militaristic campaign in my province. They cherish the hope of setting up a national federal party, which would merely be, under another name, the old tory party with which no one wishes to be associated in our province. They fondly expect a repetition of the tragedy of 1911.
There is no occasion for doubting that, belonging as we do to the British Commonwealth, even as a free and sovereign partner, we may sooner or later, have to decide whether we should bleed our country white in order to protect the empire's interests. But I do say, most emphatically that the liberals remember too well the bloody experience of 1917, that we believe our patriotism to be at least as sincere as the patriotism of those worthy writers who may be publishing reputed newspapers; that, conscious of our responsibilities as representatives of the people who do not want war we are against any such venture, and that, as long as this government is in power, the Canadian people should have a feeling of security. The leader of this government took a clear cut stand when he said "Parliament will decide."
I now say to my compatriots that they need not fear to follow Mackenzie King rather than the leader of the opposition whose endeavour for military conscription in 1917 is still remembered by the people in my province.
I do say, Mr. Speaker, that such a policy is truly Canadian. That is how our beloved country has gained in international matters, the respect of other powers. Of such achieve-
The Address-Mr. Lalonde

ments is history made and future generations will find in it the record of a steadfast man who was a genuine Canadian.
Of course, an increase in the national defence estimates is forecast in the speech from the throne. I shall purposely withhold my opinion, but I understand that the Government will deal with the matter in the light of our financial resources and of the geographical position of Canada.
I now wish to congratulate the leader of the government on the very fine speech which he delivered last Monday. On that occasion the two leaders have tried conclusions. The right hon. the Prime Minister has fulfilled the expectations of connoisseurs in besting his opponent with his unimpeachable arguments, his rousing dynamism and the moderate tone of his remarks. The maiden speech of the Conservative leader was awaited with much interest in Ottawa. Being the successor of one of the most aristocratic and' well informed parliamentarians he owed it to his followers to rise at least to the heights of eloquence and sophistry where the former Tory leader had soared. It should be admitted that his task was indeed tremendous. Let me say right now that the present leader of the opposition has completely failed. He has disappointed his own followers. He has gladdened his opponents. Where his predecessor was trenchant and curt, the new leader has been vague. While the former resorted to sound reasoning, the new Conservative leader has discarded logic and delivered a speech replete with irrelevant puns and anecdotes. While the former could put the speech from the throne to a thorough analysis which sometimes led to sophistical conclusions cleverly clothed with a semblance of common sense, the latter has only touched lightly upon that piece of parliamentary oratory which is persistently referred to as the speech from the throne without extracting therefrom anything substantial.
Then the liberal leader replied. It was a triumph for him. Never within living memory had he attained those sublime heights, in such a spontaneous, moving and complete manner. Realizing his superiority over the man who had just failed in his task and summoning all the eloquence at his command, he dazzled the entire house. The leader of the opposition had reproached the liberal leader with being ignorant of the plight of the people and having never endured the suffering of the toiling and despairing masses. He had stung the lion to the quick. With sparkling eyes, with menacing gestures and in ringing tones, the liberal leader described with sobs in his voice the hardships of his forefathers, obscure heroes of pioneer days, valiant knights of the primitive exiles, who

have inscribed on the portals of our country their heroic deeds. And when he spoke of his dear old mother, whom he so dearly loves, his indignation rang in thunderous words hurled at the conservative leader. He had avenged the honour of his name, he had avenged his party. He had wiped out the insult.
Under the guidance of such men, I have no reason to doubt, much less to betray. Rather is it my duty to implore the coming generation to follow in the luminous path beaten by them.
Let them not be guided by false gods and false doctrines. Has not past experience taught us that the Liberal party of Laurier and of King has always been the beacon indicating the true road? Has not the political liberalism that we uphold always been the real liberating doctrine? Does not history teach us-and how truly!-that each Liberal administration since 1867 has restored to Canadians a certain amount of happiness and prosperity by combating the evil effects of protectionist nationalism and tearing away piece by piece from the Tory oligarchy the remnants of Canadian liberties.
Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in supporting the resolution moved by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews), which eloquently sets forth the record of a truly Canadian government led by men who have no other earthly ideal but to give the best of themselves to their country and to their fellow-men.
Mr. DENTON MASSEY (Greenwood) r Mr. Speaker, I am happy to make my first words those of congratulation to both the mover and the seconder of the motion at present before the house. I am sure that we all listened to the speeches of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews) and the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier), appreciating not only their ability but their agility to speak so well when there is so little they could say. We all admired particularly the synchromesh ease with which the hon. member for Stormont changed from one language to the other. I am sure that all the congratulations that have been showered upon him this week have been absolutely sincere.
My second words are words of congratulation to my hon. leader (Mr. Manion). I offer congratulations to him not only upon his election to the leadership of the National Conservative party of Canada, but upon assuming his position as Leader of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition. We regard ourselves as being peculiarly fortunate in having a man of his calibre as our leader, whose

The Address-Mr. Massey
record as a Canadian is as distinct as it is distinguished. He has made a magnificent contribution to Canada both in time of war and in time of peace, and his presence in this house brings to it that which alone his own presence can bring.
I would congratulate him further upon his maiden speech as leader of the opposition. All of us who listened to him last Monday realized that his absence from the house for three years had served to sharpen rather than to dull the edge of his sword. We admired the forthrightness of his presentation. He did not dodge points by the recognized device of verbiage, but his presentation was forthright and to the point, and the acclaim that it received from Halifax to Victoria is one of which he must be duly proud.
My next words are in connection with an event to which we all in this country look forward. We are happy and proud that Their Majesties the King and Queen are to visit Canada this May. From coast to coast they will receive a welcome of spontaneous loyalty and devotion from those who live in this dominion. We are proud, yes, and happy, yes; and we anticipate that we may be able to demonstrate to their majesties that Canada as a dominion in the family of empire remains in the position where she has always been.
This evening, Mr. Speaker, I am fully conscious of the necessity of discussing some of the major problems that are confronting this dominion; but it is not my purpose tonight to ventilate my views and opinions on matters which have already been discussed at some length by those who have spoken before me. There is still plenty of time and opportunity before this session is completed for me to present what I feel to be the views of my constituents on all these vitally important matters.
To-night I wish to deal particularly with one matter which is of farther reaching importance than many are apt to consider, a matter which strikes at the very roots of the liberty which we enjoy in this country and for which our forefathers fought and bled. I do not wish to appear platitudinous; but let us remind ourselves that the liberty and freedom we enjoy includes the right of free speech, free assembly, free association, and free worship. For centuries these rights have been our priceless privileges. They have become basic in our scheme of things. By no possible stretch of the imagination can they be considered to be a policy of this or of any other government; for they are fundamental to our democracy, and any abridgement of
these principles strikes a blow which is directed at the bedrock upon which our nation and our empire have been built. They are principles the practice of which is a privilege and the equal right of all free men, whether their means be mediocre or whether their means be great. They are principles that apply equally to all citizens.
As a citizen of Canada I respect those rights regardless of who exercises them. As one in public life I may protest with all the energy of which I am capable against what my opponent has to say; but I will protest equally against any curtailment of his right to say it. When we speak of free speech we are speaking of liberty, which is the inalienable right of all citizens of Canada and of Great Britain. It is only when that liberty is grossly abused to the extent of licence that any restrictions upon it should be tolerated at all.
I postulate, Mr. Speaker, that this is the principle which has motivated the action of successive governments in Canada from confederation down to the present day-the present day, when we are faced with the first example of the restriction of free speech, if not directed, at least condoned by this government in general and by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in particular in his speech on Monday last.
The argument that I am about to present deals with this principle, and may that be noted. It has nothing whatsoever to do with any particular individual

let me make that clear beyond peradventure of a doubt.
The particular instance of which I am about to speak concerns a man who notoriously and rather recently has attacked me bitterly both in his paper and on the air. I have no axe to grind for Mr. George McCullagh, or his Globe and Mail, as I have already said it was just over a year ago that he launched his attack on me, and I in return attacked his policies and his newspaper with no small degree of fervour. Let it further be noted that I have no knowledge whatsoever of what Mr. Me-Cullagh has in mind to say in his next four scheduled broadcasts, no more than I had any knowledge whatsoever of what he was going to say in his first broadcast.
Still further let me state that my criticisms are directed against no one individual; that I have the highest personal regard for those who are directly responsible for the present situation. May I say that my own personal dealings with the broadcasting corporation, its officers and government representative, have been of the happiest. Thus it is that I am virtually amazed at this recent turn of events. It has been my pleasure to have
The Address-Mr. Massey

many dealings with the broadcasting corporation, and my regard for its officers and its government representative has sprung from actual experience. In many ways I feel that the management of the broadcasting corporation are to be heartily congratulated upon their efforts to date; but the recent action on their part, which has received so much publicity not only throughout Canada but throughout the United States and Great Britain as well, cannot be allowed to go unchallenged by those of us who sit in this house.
Let me review briefly, Mr. Speaker, the events that took place between Mr. Mc-Cullagh and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation during the last two weeks or so. On January 3 Mr. George McCullagh, publisher of the Globe and Mail, applied for the use of the national network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in order to present to the public of Canada in a wider way than was possible through his newspaper the views of his paper concerning matters of public interest. He was to broadcast as publisher of the Globe and Mail, and not as an individual, the newspaper to use him as their air mouthpiece. Mr. McCullagh telephoned his request to Major Gladstone Murray, explaining to him the nature of the talks that were to be given, and stating his willingness and preparedness to submit his script in advance for approval. It was pointed out by Major Murray in a letter confirming the telephone conversation, that Mr. McCullagh's application could not be accepted, and it was suggested that he take part in the corporation's Sunday evening forum, which would require him to accept the subject allotted to him and to speak for fourteen minutes on one occasion. Mr. McCullagh wrote Major Murray on January 4 protesting and making his application anew. The following day Major Murray replied in a letter which quoted rulings recently approved by the board of governors, including this. I quote:
No individual may purchase network broadcasts for his own opinions.
It is important to note that in this letter Major Murray also observed:
These rulings which apply also to individual CBC stations but not individual privately owned stations, were the subject of most careful consideration.
Surely it is obvious from this statement in the general manager's own words-I am not using mine-that under the policy of the corporation time could be booked on privately owned stations for the broadcast of individual opinions. In accordance with this obvious conclusion, confirmed by Major Murray's letter of January 5, Mr. McCullagh proceeded to

secure time on all the privately owned stations in Ontario, nineteen in number, I believe, for the period from five to five-thirty p.m. on Sunday afternoons for a series of five broadcasts to commence on January 15. On January 6, Mr. McCullagh received a further communication from Major Murray suggesting that he participate in a forum with Professor Taylor, of McMaster university, on the prosy subject, "Canadian trade-in what direction?" Mr. McCullagh replied to the effect that there were many problems which he wanted to discuss and that he did not wish to be limited and governed by an academic subject handed to him by any corporate body of the government. He further informed the corporation that he intended to broadcast over the available privately owned stations in Ontario,-which was, of course, as I have noted, in accordance with Major Murray's letter of January 5. On January 12, Major Murray again wrote Mr. McCullagh, and from that letter I quote the following paragraph:
While the whole matter of private stations network is under review the board of governors has instructed that no permission for new commitments on non-basic networks shall be granted until at least the board has received the representations of private stations at the next board meeting which is expected to take place about the middle of March.
Let it be noted that as late as Thursday, January 12, three days before his first scheduled broadcast, Mr. McCullagh was denied the use of the privately owned Ontario stations on a non-basic network. Here, I postulate, was a new ruling on the part of the board of governors of the broadcasting corporation, and it is frankly so admitted in Major Murray's letter, for he says that this matter will not be under review until the middle of March.
I state here that no such occurrence has taken place before in the history of Canadian broadcasting and accordingly it appears clear that for some reason discrimination has been shown against Mr. McCullagh. That is the only possible interpretation of the action taken.
Feeling that a gross injustice had been done to him, Mr. McCullagh found a means of circumventing the restriction of freedom of speech by the corporation, and placed his speech upon wax and distributed the discs to the privately owned stations that were not permitted to be tied up in a non-basic network, while he himself conducted a live broadcast from the single station CFRB. I listened with particular care last Sunday afternoon to Mr. McCullagh's remarks. I have before me a verbatim copy of those remarks. The address was, I suggest, of

The Address-Mr. Massey
definite and great interest to the people of Canada. It attacked no one in particular, but it challenged the people of Canada to attain to better government through determined action. His efforts were obviously directed to arouse the electorate to build up responsible government and demand courageous leadership. Whereas he was not very complimentary to any one of us in this house, no one can say that his speech was either damaging or destructive, but on the contrary it was constructive and will without doubt do good.
This statement, may I again remind hon. members, is coming from one who is a prejudiced witness in regard to Mr. McCullagh, for the last time when Mr. McCullagh was on the air, a year ago, he vigorously attacked me personally. No matter what Mr. McCullagh said; no matter who Mr. McCullagh is; no matter what Mr. McCullagh represents, I repeat that the broadcasting corporation has assumed and taken unto itself rights never in the world given to it under the Canadian Broadcasting Act of 1936. When I make that statement I know whereof I speak. As the Prime Minister reminded me when I took the liberty of interrupting him when he was speaking on Monday evening, I was on the committee which submitted the report from which the bill was drawn, and that report passed the committee unanimously. But I certainly had no thought in my mind that such an action would be taken based on the legislation drafted from the report of that committee.
I think we have covered certain phases of this subject, perhaps a bit hurriedly and perhaps not completely; but I do feel, and feel very definitely, that an injustice has been done Mr. McCullagh, and therefore I hesitate not at all to bring this matter to the attention of the house.
I should like to say further that not so very long ago-I believe it was under date of January 14-the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) was interviewed by that very able correspondent in Ottawa of the Toronto Daily Star, Mr. Robert Lipsett. I have in my hand the Star of January 14, in which there is a report of the interview with the minister. May I summarize what the minister had to say to Mr. Lipsett:
1.	. . . Nor was the application of existing regulations in his, Mr. McCulIagh's, case any different from what it was in at least twenty previous instances.
2.	It is a fundamental principle applied everywhere where there is network broadcasting that no individual may purchase time on any network to broadcast his Own opinions.
3.	A privilege granted to Mr. McCullagh could not be withheld from others, nor could a privilege denied others be granted to Mr. McCullagh.
4.	The government had nothing to do with the decision on Mr. McCulIagh's application. "I did not learn of it until I received a copy of the correspondence from Major Murray."
In the first instance, the minister states that this case is no different from at least twenty previous instances. He cited one case in particular, that of a broadcast which was to be delivered by Sir Edward Beatty, permission for which was refused. I regret to say for the minister's sake that Sir Edward Beatty saw fit to deny this statement and stated that he knew of no such instance in his own experience; and it is rather unfortunate that the minister selected that case. Sir Edward further reminded his interviewer that on several occasions he had broadcast addresses coast to coast over CBC stations. I urge the minister, if he cares to reply to this speech, to give to the house his other nineteen "instances."
The Minister of Transport also stated that wherever there is network broadcasting no individual can purchase time on any network to broadcast his own opinions. Well, of course that statement is absurd, absurd because it is untrue. Such regulations may exist; but the minister knows this, that, if so, they certainly have not been carried out in Canada and the United States. Time and time again in both countries this has been the case. Let me quote section 326 of the United States radio law of 1934, which is in effect to-day:
Nothing in this act shall be understood or construed to give the federal commission the power of censorship over the radio communications or signals transmitted by any radio station, or no regulation shall be promulgated or fixed by the commission which shall interfere with the right of free speech by means of radio communication.
Contrast the Canadian point of view that we have had manifest in the last few days with that held by the United States. It was a matter of interest to the Toronto Daily Star, and accordingly they had a reporter in New York city make several calls on the broadcasting station headquarters. In reporting the interview, the reporter, on January 16, asked a question of the heads of one of the broadcasting companies:
"Suppose the publisher of the New York Herald Tribune wanted to buy time, would you sell it?"
"I doubt very much we'd sell it," said Mr. Babb of NBC, "but we'd give it."
They would be willing to have a responsible individual broadcast, so far willing as to give him the time. The minister has only to look
The Address-Mr. Massey

across the border to the United States to find there the example of Rev. Father Coughlin who, every Sunday afternoon, broadcasts from the Shrine of the Little Flower his personal views which are aired over a network of forty-six United States stations and for which he pays. I have in my hand a copy of a statement that appeared on the front page of the Globe and Mail on Monday last in which he said he broadcasts over a network of forty-six stations. Father Coughlin further says in part:
"I would not care to comment on the situation you have outlined to me," he told a reporter, "but' if Mr. McCullagh should ever find himself unable to reach a broad enough audience through Canadian stations he will be welcome to use this chain at any time."
To compare the policy of the British Broadcasting Corporation with the policy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in this regard is also absurd. The question of the airing of opinion cannot possibly arise in Great Britain because the British Broadcasting Corporation is simply not in commercial business, sells no time. It is not on a commercial basis but is self-supporting, and therefore a situation such as has arisen here could not possibly arise there.
Let us come back to Canada. I give the minister the example of Colonel George Drew who as recently as last November repeatedly aired his opinions to the province of Ontario through an Ontario network. At that time Colonel Drew was merely a private citizen, an individual holding no office whatsoever in any political party. Now, the most amazing example of all, which shows, I think, that there must have been some discrimination against Mr. McCullagh, more clearly than any that could be given. He had been sold a network before. He was sold a network in October, 1937, and he broadcast over a number of Ontario stations! He was just as much an individual then as he is now. Why should he be able to broadcast in 1937 at the height of an election campaign, if he cannot broadcast now? Can it possibly be that in 1937, in his broadcasts, he was obviously going to support the Liberal party in Ontario, whereas in 1939 it was presumed by many that he would attack the present Liberal government at Ottawa?
Let us recall the statement made by the Prime Minister in the course of his remarks on Monday. He used this language, which will be found at page 12 of Hansard:
I simply wish to say that the government has had nothing whatever to do with refusing any application that has been made to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Neither the government nor any member of the government had any knowledge that an application had been made to the Canadian Broadcasting Cor-

poration by the publisher of one of Toronto's leading newspapers, nor had any member of the government any knowledge that such an application had been refused.
As lion, members know, the business of controlling and regulating radio broadcasting has been placed by this parliament under the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which is an autonomous public body and with which the government does not interfere and has no desire to interfere.
Does the Prime Minister mean to tell the people of Canada that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has not only the power to execute a policy but, further, the right to establish a principle which affects the basic foundation upon which this country has been built, a principle which touches the very quick centre of our national life? Has any department of this government the power to restrict the time-honoured rights of the individual

free speech, free assembly, free association, free worship, or anything else to which the individual is entitled? Is any department, commission, corporation or company, responsible to the government of Canada, and owned by the Canadian people, free to upset established principles without any question on the part of the government? Yet that is exactly what has happened.
The action of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is extraordinary from many points of view. Do hon. members realize that the decision taken in regard to the McCullagh matter by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation denies to the individual a privilege that is enjoyed by our political parties in Canada? If Mr. McCullagh claimed membership in a party instead of professing independence, as he does, he could without any question obtain time on a coast-to-coast network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. But as he is an individual he is denied that right, a right which would be his were he a party man. What skinny justice is here? Let those who state that just because he has a wealthy organization behind him Mr. McCullagh should be denied the privilege of broadcasting his opinion, consider the accepted practice of the various broadcasting companies including the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation every Sunday evening carries the Ford hour, which brings to the listeners of Canada the delightful music of the Detroit symphony orchestra.

speechtext:
Thank you, your honour, for the courtesy. The purpose of the broadcast in question, the Ford hour, is to air vigorous political opinions.
Again, a short time ago, one of the wealthiest corporations in Canada. General Motors of Canada, Limited, purchased time on a coast-to-coast network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. For what purpose? To permit the airing of Mr. Beverley Baxter's personal views concerning the government and the foreign policy of the United Kingdom. That was the program.
Let us go even farther. I postulate to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who so tactfully disclaims any responsibility for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, saying that the administration of policy is entirely in the hands of the corporation, that this powerful organization, maintained by a nuisance tax on the public, is being used
for political purposes and for furthering the interests of those who sit on the treasury benches. At regular intervals this autumn radio addresses have been made by various ministers of the crown, and made at the public expense; and in my opinion these addresses in great part have been little more than cunningly-designed political speeches, in an attempt to show the country, in spite of what the public may think, that these ministers after all are really capable men. I have endeavoured to obtain copies of these speeches to make quotations from them in order to justify the point I have just made, that they are political in character. Unfortunately, according to my information, the printed word will not be available for another fortnight.
In his speech on Monday night, however, the Prime Minister himself admitted that he could use the radio when he wished to do so. Let us listen to his words, as they appear at page 66 of Hansard-.
-the Prime Minister of Canada cannot be going back and forth across the country making political speeches and making personal appearances before local audiences. He has this House of Commons to speak in. What better forum is there in the world? He has the radio to speak over. Is it not much better to give a few nation-wide addresses in carefully chosen words-
Then I am afraid the right hon. gentleman did not become very complimentary, but I am sure he was facetious.
[DOT]-than to be given the kind of oration to which we have listened this afternoon and to-night?
Then too, at the public expense there comes blasting into our homes a forum conducted by various individuals, college professors and other men. I have listened to many of these forums. Some of them have been passably good; others have been ridiculous, and some have been fatuous. Still others have been destructive, irritably and irrationally anti-empire, iso-lationistic and bound to do harm rather than good in these days when Canadian unity is being so severely tried.
As I come to the conclusion of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, let me again impress upon hon. members that my purpose in taking up the time of the house this evening on this matter has nothing whatsoever to do with Mr. McCullagh as an individual, or his Globe and Mail as a newspaper. I am not concerned with what Mr. McCullagh has to say or what he thinks; but I am concerned, as I think every member of this house should be, when we lodge power in any one man or any small group of men to pass on one of the basic principles upon which this country has been established. And I am further concerned when one of the ministers of the crown, to
The Address-Mr. Massey

whom this body is responsible, washes his hands of the matter and says, "This has nothing to do with me. It is a question of policy for the corporation." I am also concerned when the Prime Minister of Canada himself, who has made such eloquent speeches on constitutional rights and constitutional authority, disclaims any responsibility for the action of a body appointed by his government which abridges these rights, and makes the amazing statement in this house that he is prepared to back up that action. Let me quote from page 14 of Hansard:
Mr. Woodsworth:	May we not have the
assurance of the Prime Minister that the
fovernment will stand behind the Canadian iroadcasting Corporation in this matter?
Mr. Mackenzie King:	I think so, yes.
That is a typical answer from the Prime Minister.
Just because a man may be possessed of a substantial quantity of this world's goods is no reason why his rights should be abridged or his voice unheard. Surely those who discredit this point of view are inconsistent when under the dictates of their worthy desire for justice they champion the right of free speech for him who is not so well to do-and all power to them in their effort-but why in the name of justice should they wish to restrict the right of him who happens to be well to do? I am firmly of the opinion that free speech is the right of any man, be he well to do or possessed of the most modest means. It amounts to this: Either we have free speech in Canada or we have not. Either we have free assembly or we have not. Either we have a free press or we have not. Either we have free association or we have not. Either we have free worship or we have not.
May it be remembered that there was a committee which submitted a report from which the present broadcasting act was drafted. I sat on that committee, and I know what was the purpose in the minds of those who approved that report. I postulate that the present action of the corporation goes far beyond the intent of that act, as admitted by the general manager of the corporation himself when he said that to settle this matter there would be a meeting of the board of governors in March. The corporation was to administer policy, yes; to administer policy independent of but subject to review by the Minister of Transport, yes; but to establish principle? No; a thousand times no!

Before I take my seat, let me point out that the matters which have been dealt with in the speech from the throne, and with which I purpose to deal from time to time during the session, are matters to which I am by no means insensible this evening. Let it not be said I have neglected them; for I shall deal with them, as I stated in opening, from time to time during this session. Let me now merely state, Mr. Speaker, that I am supporting whole-heartedly the amendment moved by my leader to the motion that is before this house. I shall not support the amendment to the amendment, which is designed cleverly and adroitly by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Woods-worth), who moved it.
I oppose monopolistic control and exploitation just as heartily as any member of this house, and despise it in principle and in result, but I shall vote against the amendment to the amendment for the obvious reason that a vote for it, as it is worded, would be a vote in favour of socialism in Canada, and that I do not support.
I thank your honour, hon. members in general, and my hon. friend the right hon.
